name: Kindergarten
theme: God loves me and made me

units.title: God made everything
units.eq: Who made the world, and why?

lessons.title: God is our loving Father
lessons.idea: God is our Father. He is good, and he loves every one of us. He is always with us.
lessons.question: How do you know when someone loves you?
lessons.activity: Draw a picture of your family and trace a heart around it. Say, “God loves us.”
teach: Aim: every child leaves knowing “God is my Father and he loves me.” At five, trust comes before ideas; a child who feels loved by God can later pray, forgive and be brave.

Calling God Father tells us he is the source of all things and also pure goodness and loving care for his children (CCC 239). Jesus taught us to say “Our Father” (CCC 2779 asks us to set aside false images).
Say: “God takes care of you like a good parent, only even more, and he is always with you.” If asked “Where is God?”: “We can’t see him, but he is with us the way love is with us.”

Some children have a father who is absent, harsh or gone. Describe God by what he does (loves, listens, stays) and never ask “who is your dad?” Mention mothers and grandparents who care for them as signs of God’s love.
Ask: “Who takes care of you? What does God do for you?” Look for a child who says God loves, helps or is with them. Watch whether they can say “Our Father” in the Sign-of-the-Cross voice.
talk: Who takes care of you at home?
What does your family do when someone is sad?
What would you like to tell God today?
quiz: Who is our Father in heaven?|God|A king far away|Nobody|A statue|0|God is our loving Father.
God loves…|Only good children|Only adults|Everyone|Only the strong|2|God loves every person.

Mia is alone in the dark. What can she remember about God?|He is her Father and is with her|He watches only when she is good|He stays at church all week|He is busy helping bigger people|0|God our Father is always with us, even at night.

Why can we call God “Father”?|He is very strict and keeps a list of rules|He looks just like all the dads we know|He loves and cares for us|He is the Father of grown-ups only|2|God is like a loving father, only more.

Tom yelled at his sister and feels bad. What is true?|God picked a different child|God is far away from him now|God is still his loving Father|God loves him less for a while|2|God is always our loving Father.
lessons.life: At bedtime this week, say together: “God, thank you for loving us.”
lessons.saint: Thérèse of Lisieux: a little girl who loved God as her Father and trusted him in everything.
lessons.mem: God is my Father and he loves me.
lessons.hook: Hold a child’s picture of their own father or caregiver. Ask, “Who takes care of you?” Then say, “God takes care of you even more.”
lessons.assess: Ask each child to finish: “God is my Father, and he…”

script.open: Sit in a circle. Hold up a photo of a family (yours or a picture-book family) and say, “Who takes care of this family? Who makes sure they have food, and a bed, and a hug?” Let three children answer. Then say, “Today we are going to meet Someone who takes care of everyone in the whole world.”
teach: Say: “We have a mommy and a daddy, or a grandma, or someone at home who takes care of us. But there is Someone even bigger. His name is God. Jesus told us we can call him Father. That is what we say in the Our Father: ‘Our Father, who art in heaven.’”

Say: “A good father loves his children very much. He is always glad when they come to him. That is what God is like. He is good. He loves every one of us. And here is the best thing: he is always with us, even in the dark, even when we are sad, even when Mommy or Daddy is not in the room.”

Read Psalm 23:1 slowly: “The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.” Say: “A shepherd looks after his sheep. God looks after us the same way.” Hold up the picture of the Good Shepherd carrying a lamb.
ask: Who takes care of you at home? (Let each child name someone.)
What do you think God is like? (Listen for: kind, big, loves me. If a child says scary, gently say: “God is good and he loves us.”)
Where is God right now? (Listen for: everywhere, with us. Say: “Yes. He is always with us.”)
practice: Give each child paper and crayons.
Say: “Draw the people who love you. Take your time.”
While they draw, walk around and ask each child to tell you about their picture.
When most are finished, say: “Now draw a big heart all around your family. God loves every one of them. And he loves you.”
Hold up the pictures together. Say: “God loves us!” and let everyone say it back.
script.close: Stand and make the Sign of the Cross together, slowly. Say: “Father, thank you for loving us. Amen.” Send the drawings home with a note: “Tonight, tell your family: God loves us.”

tryit: Draw the people who love you.
Trace a big heart around all of them.
Say it together: “God loves us.”
lessons.saintStory:
Thérèse Martin was born in France in 1873, the youngest in a big, loving family. Her mother died when she was four, and she leaned on her father and on God very much.
She called God her Father and trusted him like a little child trusts a parent who is holding her hand. When she became a nun she wrote that she did not have to do big things. She could do small things, like smiling at a grumpy person, with great love.
Thérèse reminds us that God is not far away or scary. He is the best Father, and we can bring him everything, even the little things.

lessons.title: God made the world
lessons.idea: God made the sky, the sea, the animals and the plants. He made them because he is good. He looked and said, “It is good.”
lessons.question: What is your favorite thing God made?
lessons.activity: Go on a short nature walk, or look at photographs. Each child names one thing God made and says “Thank you, God.”
teach: Aim: the world is a gift from a good God, so we say thank you and take care of it. A child who sees creation as a gift will naturally wonder, be grateful and be gentle.
The Church professes God as Creator of heaven and earth (CCC 279). He made everything out of love, with order and wisdom (CCC 299), and nothing needed to exist except that he wanted it.
Say: “Before anything was, God was. He said it and it was, because he is God.” If a child asks “Who made God?”: “Nobody. God has always been, he had no beginning. That is what makes him God.”
Do not set Genesis against science; a five-year-old may hear dinosaurs, space or evolution at home. Say: “God made it all; people study how.” Avoid mocking any family’s view.
Walk the room naming a made thing and ask: “Who made this?” Listen for “God” and for a thank-you. Invite each child to name one creation they are thankful for.
talk: What did God make that you can see right now?
Why do you think God made so many animals?
How can we take care of what God made?
quiz: Who made the sky, sea and animals?|The wind|Nobody|People|God|3|God is the Creator.
What did God say about what he made?|It is bad|Nothing|It is boring|It is good|3|Genesis 1.

Why did God make the sky, sea and animals?|Because he is good|Because he needed some helpers on earth|Because the world just made itself|Because he was lonely in heaven|0|God made everything out of goodness.

You smell a flower on a walk. What fits best?|Say flowers just happen to grow|Say thank you to God|Tell everyone that you made it|Pick every flower you can see|1|Creation is a gift, and we say thank you.

A child asks, “If scientists study plants, did God not make them?” What is a good answer?|Scientists made them instead of God|God made only the animals and the sky|Plants made themselves long ago|God made them; scientists learn how|3|God made the world and scientists find out how it works.
lessons.life: Take a walk with your family and say “thank you, God” for three things you see.
lessons.saint: Francis of Assisi: he called the sun, the moon and the animals his brothers and sisters because God made them all.
lessons.mem: God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. (Genesis 1:31)
lessons.hook: Bring a flower, a shell and a stone in a basket. Ask, “Who made these?” Let them hold each one.
lessons.assess: Ask each child to name one thing God made and say “Thank you, God.”

script.open: Before the children arrive, put a few things from outdoors on a tray under a cloth: a leaf, a smooth stone, a feather, a pinecone or shell. Say, “I have some surprises. Each one was made by someone very wonderful.” Lift the cloth and let them touch each thing gently.
teach: Say: “Who made the leaf? A person? No! Nobody in a factory made this. God made it. God made the sky and the sea, the animals and the trees, the sun in the day and the moon at night.”

Tell the story from Genesis 1 in pieces, with a gesture for each day: light (open hands wide), sky and sea (wave arms), land and plants (grow from a crouch), sun and moon, fish and birds (fly your hands), animals and people. After each piece say with the children: “And God saw that it was good.”
Say: “Why did God make everything? Because he is good, and he wanted to share. He made it all for us to enjoy and take care of. And when we say thank you, God is very happy.”
ask: What is your favorite thing God made? (Everyone gets a turn.)
Was it a good world or a bad world when God made it? (Listen for: good! Say: “Very good.”)
How can we take care of what God made? (Listen for: water the plants, be kind to animals, not break things.)
practice: Take the children outside, or to a window, or show a few big photographs of nature.
Say: “Look with your eyes. Look at something for a long time. Find one thing God made.”
Go around the circle. Each child says, “Thank you, God, for ____.” The others answer, “Thank you, God.”
Back inside, pass around the leaf, the stone and the feather again. Say: “These are God’s gifts.”
script.close: Say the grace together: “Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts.” Make the Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Find one beautiful thing God made and say thank you.”

tryit: Look carefully at what God made.
Pick one thing and say, “Thank you, God, for ____.”
Listen to the others’ thank-yous.
lessons.saintStory:
Francis was born in Assisi, Italy, about 800 years ago. His father was a rich cloth merchant, but Francis chose to give away his fine clothes and live simply so he could follow Jesus.
Francis loved everything God made. He called the sun his brother and the moon his sister, and he wrote a song of thanks for the water, the wind and the fire. Stories say that he preached to the birds, and that animals were gentle with him.
Francis shows us that the world is a gift. When we look at a flower or a bird and say “thank you, God,” we are doing what Saint Francis did.

lessons.title: God made me
lessons.idea: God made me in a special way. I am a person, not a thing. God made me to know him and love him.
lessons.question: What can you do that animals cannot do?
lessons.activity: Trace each child’s hand on paper and write “God made me.” Display them together.
teach: Aim: each child knows “God made me on purpose and loves me just as I am.” That sense of worth protects them from comparing, bullying and shame, and it grounds all later moral teaching.
Humans are made in God’s image, a person who is someone, not something, able to know and love God (CCC 355–357). The soul and body together make one person, loved by God from the first moment.
Say: “You are not an accident. God thought of you and wanted you, and nobody else is just like you.” If asked “Why did God make me?”: “To know him, love him and be happy with him.”

Be careful with children who have disabilities, health issues, adoption or a hard family story. Never compare bodies, abilities or looks. Say “every child”, and mean it. Avoid “God made me perfect” as a comparison.
Ask: “Who made you? Does God love you?” Look for children who answer with confidence. Notice anyone who hangs back or says something negative about themselves, and affirm them privately.
talk: What are you good at?
What makes you different from your friend?
How can you show love to someone today?
quiz: Who made you?|A machine|The wind|God|Nobody|2|God made each person.
God made people to…|Be alone|Know him and love him|Fight|Be perfect|1|CCC 356.

Mia says, “I am not important.” What is true?|God wanted her on purpose|She must do great things to matter|God only makes a few very special people|She was made like a thing in a shop|0|God wanted you.

How is a person different from a toy?|A person is made of nicer things|A person has a body and a soul|A person was made just for fun|A person can move around on its own|1|People are made in God’s image with body and soul.

A boy in a wheelchair thinks he is less special. What is true?|He is special only when he can walk|Special children are made by accident|Everyone is wonderfully made|God made some people less perfect than others|2|Everyone is wonderfully made by God.
lessons.life: Look in a mirror and say, “God made me and loves me.” Do it for five days.
lessons.saint: Carlo Acutis: a boy who loved God and computers and showed that everyone has gifts.
misc: “God made some people better than others.”
lessons.mem: I am wonderfully made. (Psalm 139:14)
lessons.hook: Let children look in a mirror. Say, “Who made that wonderful face? God did!”
lessons.assess: Ask each child, “Who made you?” and “Why?” (to know and love God).

script.open: Hold up a mirror. Walk around the circle and let each child look at their own face. Say softly, “Look. There is someone God made. There is only one of them in the whole world.”
teach: Say: “When God made the animals, he said, ‘Let the earth bring forth.’ But when he made people, he did something special. He said, ‘Let us make people like us.’ God made you in a very special way, with a body and with a soul that will never die.”

Say: “You are a person, not a thing. A toy is a thing. A chair is a thing. You are somebody. Nobody else is exactly like you. God knew you before you were born. That is what the psalm says: ‘I am wonderfully made.’”
Say: “And God made you for a reason: to know him and to love him. He gave you eyes to see his world, ears to hear, hands to help, and a heart to love.”
ask: What can your hands do? (Listen for: draw, hug, wave, help. Say: “God gave you those hands to love with.”)
What is something you are good at? (Everyone shares. Make sure every child gets something good said about them.)
Is anyone else exactly like you? (Listen for: no. Say: “That is why God loves you so much. There is only one you.”)
practice: Give each child a sheet of paper and a crayon.
Help each child trace their hand with the other hand holding the crayon.
Write “God made me” inside the hand (write it lightly for the child to trace over, if you can).
Let the children decorate the hands with a favorite color.
Display the hands together on a wall. Say: “Look at all the people God made.”
script.close: Put your hand on your heart. Say: “Thank you, God, for making me.” Then the Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family one thing God made you good at.”

tryit: Trace your hand.
Write your name inside it.
Say: “God made me.”
lessons.saintStory:
Carlo Acutis was born in 1991 and grew up in Milan, Italy. He was a cheerful boy who liked soccer, video games and animals, and he loved Jesus in the Eucharist. He went to Mass almost every day.
Carlo was very good with computers. When he was a teenager, he taught himself to build websites, and he made one that showed Eucharistic miracles from all over the world, so that more people could learn about Jesus in the Eucharist. He was kind to people who were lonely and to those who had less than he did.
Carlo became very ill when he was fifteen and died in 2006. The Church has named him a saint. He shows us that God makes every child with gifts, and that a child can use their gifts to help others know God.

lessons.title: Jesus is born
lessons.idea: God sent his Son, Jesus, to be a baby. Mary was his mother and Joseph took care of him. Jesus is God, and he is also a real person.
lessons.question: Who was in the stable with baby Jesus?
lessons.activity: Act out the story with a doll and a blanket. Sing a gentle Christmas song.
teach: Aim: the child hears that God loved us so much he sent his own Son, who became a real baby. This is the heart of Christmas: Christmas is about Jesus, not only about gifts.
The Son of God became man for our salvation (CCC 456). Born in a stable to a poor family, he was first shown to humble shepherds (CCC 525). He is truly God and truly man.
Say: “Jesus is God, and he came as a baby so we could be close to him.” If asked “How can a baby be God?”: “God can do anything; he chose to be small because he loves us.”
Avoid blending the story with Santa or cartoon scenery; keep it as true history. Be aware of children whose families do not celebrate Christmas or who struggle, and keep the focus on welcome.
Ask: “Who was born? Who was his mother?” Let a child place figures in a manger. Listen for “Jesus”, “Mary” and “baby”, and see if they say Jesus is God’s Son.
talk: How do we take care of a baby?
Who came to visit Jesus?
Why do you think God sent his Son as a baby?
quiz: Who was Jesus’s mother?|Elizabeth|Martha|Anna|Mary|3|Luke 2.
Where was Jesus born?|Bethlehem|Nazareth|Rome|Egypt|0|Luke 2:4-7.

Jesus was a real baby. What else is true about him?|He was a story with no real child|He was only a very good man|He was an angel dressed as a baby|He is God’s Son and also God|3|Jesus is God and also a real person.

Why did God send his Son as a baby?|Because the world had no babies|To keep Mary from being alone|So we could know God close up|Because God had run out of ideas|2|God became a baby so we could know him.
Who took care of baby Jesus every day?|The shepherds from the hills|The angels in the sky|The innkeeper in town|Mary and Joseph|3|Mary was his mother and Joseph cared for him.
lessons.life: Put a small crib scene where your family can see it and say “Welcome, Jesus” each night.
lessons.saint: Francis of Assisi: he made the first living nativity scene to help people see how Jesus was born.
lessons.mem: Today a Savior has been born for you. (Luke 2:11)
lessons.hook: Bring a doll wrapped in a blanket. Whisper, “A very special baby was born long ago.”
lessons.assess: Ask: “Who was born at Christmas? Who took care of him?”

script.open: Bring a real baby blanket and a doll. Wrap the doll gently and say very quietly, “Shh. Come close. I want to tell you about the most special baby that ever lived.”
teach: Tell the story slowly with pauses: “A long time ago, Mary and Joseph traveled to a town called Bethlehem. There was no room at the inn. So they stayed where the animals sleep. And that night Mary’s baby was born. Her baby was Jesus. She wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger, where the animals eat.”
Say: “Shepherds were out in the fields. Angels came! They sang, ‘Glory to God in the highest!’ The shepherds hurried to Bethlehem and found baby Jesus, just as the angel said.”
Say: “Here is the greatest secret. This baby is God’s own Son. God came to be a real baby, so that he could be close to us. Jesus is God, and he is also a real person, like us.”
ask: Where was Jesus born? (Listen for: Bethlehem, where the animals were, a stable.)
Who came to see Jesus? (Shepherds, angels, Joseph and Mary.)
Why did God send his Son as a baby? (Listen for: because he loves us, to be with us.)
practice: Choose children to be Mary, Joseph and the shepherds, and a few to be the angels. The doll is baby Jesus.
Narrate the story again slowly. Children do the actions: walk to Bethlehem, knock on doors, kneel at the manger.
Everyone sings softly (“Away in a Manger,” or any gentle carol) while Mary and Joseph hold baby Jesus.
Rotate roles so that every child gets a part.
script.close: Say the first line of the Hail Mary together: “Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee.” Make the Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Put baby Jesus in your nativity scene tonight.”

tryit: Listen to the story of Jesus’ birth.
Act it out with the doll and the blanket.
Sing softly to baby Jesus.
lessons.saintStory:
Francis of Assisi wanted to help people see what Christmas really means. In December 1223, in the little town of Greccio in Italy, he asked a friend to set up a manger with straw, with an ox and a donkey beside it.
On Christmas night the villagers came with torches and candles, and a priest said Mass at the manger. People said they felt as if they were standing at Bethlehem. This is how the first nativity scene came to be, and why we still set one up at Christmas.
Francis loved that Jesus, who is God, became a tiny baby for us. When we look at our nativity scene, we can feel what the people of Greccio felt.

lessons.title: Jesus loves children
lessons.idea: Jesus loved the children and held them in his arms. Jesus loves you right now.
lessons.question: How would it feel to sit on Jesus’ lap?
lessons.activity: Retell the story with felt pieces. Give each child a turn to say, “Jesus loves me.”
teach: Aim: each child hears “Jesus wants me, and I am welcome to him.” Young children often feel they must be quiet or good first; the Gospel shows Jesus welcoming them as they are.
Jesus welcomed children and said the kingdom belongs to those who receive it like a child (Mark 10:13–16). Childlike trust is the model for prayer (CCC 2785, 526).
Say: “Jesus is happy when you come to him. You don’t have to be perfect.” If asked “Is Jesus here now?”: “Yes, he is with us always, and we meet him in prayer and the Mass.”
Some children feel unwanted, move between homes or have been told they are bad. Use warm eye contact, learn each name and avoid singling anyone out as the “good” child. Hold the story gently.
Ask each child, “Does Jesus love you?” and watch for smiles or a yes. Ask what Jesus did with the children; they should say he hugged or blessed them, not sent them away.
talk: How did the children feel when Jesus hugged them?
What do you want to say to Jesus?
How can you be kind to the little children at your house?
quiz: What did Jesus do with the children?|Ignored them|Blessed them|Sent them away|Scolded them|1|Mark 10:16.
Jesus loves…|Only good children|Children too|Only grown-ups|Nobody|1|Jesus welcomes children.

Grown-ups said, “Jesus is too busy for children.” What did Jesus do?|Told the children to wait outside|Agreed and sent them home|Welcomed them and held them close|Blessed only the oldest ones|2|Jesus welcomed children and held them.

Sam thinks Jesus loves him only when he is good. What is true?|Jesus loves him right now|Jesus loved children long ago only|Jesus loves him once he says sorry|Jesus loves only well-behaved kids|0|Jesus loves each child right now.

Why does it matter that Jesus knew the children by name?|He had a short list of favorites|He was only being polite|He wanted to look important|He loves each child one by one|3|Jesus’ love is for each one by name.
lessons.life: Give someone at home a hug and say “Jesus loves you.”
lessons.saint: Bl. Laura Vicuña: a young girl who loved Jesus and prayed for her mother.
misc: “Only grown-ups can be close to God.”
lessons.mem: Let the children come to me. (Mark 10:14)
lessons.hook: Hold up a picture of Jesus with children. Ask, “How do you think the children felt?”
lessons.assess: Ask each child to say, “Jesus loves me.”

script.open: Sit on the floor, not in a chair, and ask the children to sit close. Say, “Today’s story is about a time when some grown-ups said to the children, ‘Go away, Jesus is too busy.’ Do you think he was too busy?”
teach: Tell it: “One day, parents brought their children to Jesus so that he could bless them. The friends of Jesus, called disciples, said, ‘Don’t bother him. He is tired.’ But Jesus was not happy. He said, ‘Let the children come to me. Don’t stop them.’”
Say: “Then Jesus took the children in his arms. He put his hands on them. And he blessed them. Can you imagine what that was like? Jesus looked at each child with love.”

Say: “Jesus loves children. That means he loves you, right now. He loves you when you are happy and he loves you when you cry. He loves you when you are good and when you make a mistake. He is never too busy for you.”
ask: What did the friends of Jesus say? (They said to send the children away.) What did Jesus say? (Let them come!)
How did Jesus show he loved the children? (He held them and blessed them.)
What would you say to Jesus if he picked you up? (Take every answer. Say: “You can tell him anything. He always listens.”)
practice: Set out felt pieces: Jesus, a few children, some grown-ups, a path.
Retell the story, placing pieces as you tell it. Let children move the pieces.
Go around: each child holds the Jesus piece, gives it a hug, and says, “Jesus loves me.”
Everyone sits in a circle. Say: “Jesus loves you. Jesus loves you. Jesus loves every one of you.” Touch each child’s head lightly as you say it, with a blessing.
script.close: Sign of the Cross. Say: “Jesus, thank you for loving us. Amen.” Send home: “Ask someone at home to tell you how much Jesus loves you.”

tryit: Listen to the story of Jesus and the children.
Use the felt pieces to tell it back.
Say, “Jesus loves me.”
lessons.saintStory:
Laura Vicuña was born in Chile in 1891. Her father died when she was very small, and her family was very poor. Her mother had to work for a man who was not good to her.
Laura went to a school run by sisters and learned to love Jesus very much. She prayed every day for her mother. She wanted her mother to come back to the Church and to be happy. Laura offered her life to God for her mother’s sake. She died when she was only twelve.
Shortly before she died, her mother promised to change her life. Laura’s story shows us that a child’s prayers are strong, and that Jesus listens to children.

lessons.title: Jesus helps and heals
lessons.idea: Jesus helped people who were sick and sad. He still helps us today. We can ask him for help.
lessons.question: Who can we ask Jesus to help?
lessons.activity: Make “thank you” cards for a sick person. Pray together for them.
teach: Aim: the child learns Jesus cares about people who are hurting and that we can bring our needs to him. Compassion and trust in prayer begin with this simple picture.
Jesus’ healings are signs that the kingdom has come and that he is sent by the Father (CCC 547–548). They call us to faith; they do not promise that every illness will go away now.

Say: “Jesus cares when we are sick or sad, and we can tell him. He is always with us.” If asked “Why doesn’t Jesus heal Grandma?”: “I don’t know all God’s ways, but he loves her, and we can keep praying.”

Do not promise a cure or imply sickness means a lack of faith. Children may have a seriously ill parent or sibling; keep the focus on Jesus’ presence and prayer. Tell the parents if a child opens up about a deep fear.
Ask: “Who can we ask when we are sick or sad?” Invite a short prayer for someone they know. Look for children who name a person to pray for and who say Jesus helps.
talk: Who do you know who is sick?
How can we help them?
Why did only one man come back to say thank you?
quiz: Jesus helps people who are…|Strong|Sick and sad|Famous|Rich|1|Mark 1:29-34.
When Jesus helps us, we say…|Later|Thank you|Nothing|Go away|1|Luke 17:15-16.
Ana is sick and sad. What can she do?|Hide how she feels from him|Pray only when she feels good|Ask Jesus for help in prayer|Wait until she is all better first|2|We can ask Jesus for help.

Why did Jesus touch and heal sick people?|He loved them|He had nothing else to do that day|He was paying them back for something|He wanted to become very famous|0|Jesus helped people because he loves them.

A girl’s grandpa is sick. What is a good thing to say?|“Sick people are being punished”|“Jesus will fix him tomorrow, for sure”|“Praying will not help anyway”|“We can pray for him”|3|We pray for the sick without promising how God will answer.
lessons.life: Pray this week for someone who is sick, and make them a card.
lessons.saint: Damien of Molokai: a priest who cared for people with leprosy.
misc: “If I pray, everyone gets well right away.”
lessons.mem: Thank you, Jesus, for helping us.
lessons.hook: Put a bandage on a doll. Ask, “How do we help someone who’s hurt?” Then say, “Jesus helped people too.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to say one person they can pray for.

script.open: Come in with a bandage on one finger, and walk slowly. Say, “Ow. I have a little hurt. Has anyone ever felt sick or sad? What helped you feel better?” Let a few children answer.
teach: Say: “Jesus helped many people. Once, a man was very sick. His skin hurt. Everyone stayed away. But Jesus did not. He touched the sick man, and the man was made well! (Mark 1.) Jesus made sick people well, and he comforted people who were sad.”
Say: “Once Jesus healed ten men who were sick. Only one came back and said thank you. Jesus was glad he said it. (Luke 17.) When someone helps us, we say thank you.”
Say: “Jesus is still alive. He still helps us. When we are sick or sad, we can ask him for help. And sometimes he helps us by sending a mom, a dad, a nurse or a friend.”
ask: How did Jesus help people? (He healed and comforted them.)
What do we say when someone helps us? (Thank you.)
Who helps you when you are sick? (Mom, doctor, nurse. Say: “Jesus sends them.”)
practice: Hand out folded cards, crayons and stickers.
Say: “Think of someone who is sick, or sad, or lonely. Draw a happy picture for them. We will say thank you to Jesus for helping.”
Help each child write (or you write) “Jesus loves you” on the inside, and the child’s name.
Gather the cards in a basket in the middle. Pray together for the people who will receive them.
script.close: Say: “Thank you, Jesus, for helping us. Please help the people who are sick.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Give the card to someone and give them a hug.”

tryit: Think of someone who is sick or sad.
Make a thank-you card for them.
Pray for them together.
lessons.saintStory:
Damien de Veuster was born in Belgium in 1840. He became a priest and sailed across the ocean to the islands of Hawaii.
On the island of Molokai, people who had a disease called leprosy were sent to live apart, because everyone was afraid of catching it. Father Damien went to live with them. He built homes and a church, dug graves, bandaged sores and said Mass. He did not stay far away. He ate with them and touched them with love.
After some years Damien caught the disease himself, and he died in 1889. He showed that when someone is sick or sad, Jesus wants us to be close, and to help.

lessons.title: Mary is Jesus’ mother
lessons.idea: Mary said yes to God. She is Jesus’ mother and our mother too. She helps us love Jesus.
lessons.question: What do you do when your mom asks you to help?
lessons.activity: Say the first part of the Hail Mary together. Draw Mary and baby Jesus.
teach: Aim: the child meets Mary as the mother who said yes to God, and who is also a mother to us. A trusting yes to God is a model for a child’s everyday obedience and love.
Mary is the mother of Jesus and so Mother of God; the Church honors her as our mother in the order of grace (CCC 495, 501, 963). We honor her and do not worship her; worship is for God alone.
Say: “Mary loves you like a mother and she brings you to Jesus.” If asked “Is Mary God?”: “No, Mary is Jesus’ mother and our mother. She is a person like us, and God gave her a special job.”
Some Christian families do not pray to Mary, and some children have lost a mother. Speak simply and invitingly, not defensively, and let Mary be a gift, never a requirement.
Ask: “What did Mary say to the angel?” Look for “yes”. Pray the first line of the Hail Mary together and see who joins in unprompted.
talk: What did Mary say to the angel?
When did you say “yes” to someone who asked for help?
What do you do when your mom asks you to help?
quiz: Who told Mary she would be Jesus’s mother?|A neighbor|A shepherd|An angel|A king|2|Luke 1:26-38.
What did Mary say to God?|Nothing|Yes|No|Maybe|1|Luke 1:38.

Why do we love Mary so much?|She was a queen of a faraway land|She lived her whole life without worries|She is more powerful than Jesus is|She said yes to God|3|Mary said yes to God and is our mother.
How does Mary help us?|She leads us closer to Jesus|She does our hard work for us|She keeps Jesus for herself alone|She stays away from people who sin|0|Mary helps us love Jesus.

Mary was surprised by the angel. What did she do?|She said no because she was scared|She told the angel to ask another woman|She trusted God and said yes|She asked for more time to decide|2|Mary said yes to God.
lessons.life: This week, when someone asks for help, say “Yes!” with a smile and think of Mary.
lessons.saint: Juan Diego: he said yes when Mary asked him to carry her message.
misc: “We pray to Mary instead of Jesus.”
lessons.mem: Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee.
lessons.hook: Say, “Mary was a young girl who listened to an angel.” Hold up a picture of Mary.
lessons.assess: Ask: “What did Mary say to the angel?” (Yes).

script.open: Show a picture of a mother holding her baby. Ask, “Who is holding the baby?” Then show a picture of Mary and Jesus and say, “This mother is very special. She is the mother of Jesus.”
teach: Tell: “One day the angel Gabriel came to a young woman named Mary. He said, ‘Mary, God has chosen you to be the mother of his Son.’ Mary was surprised. She asked a question. And then she said, ‘Yes. Let it be done to me as you say.’ That was her ‘yes.’”
Say: “Because Mary said yes, Jesus was born. Mary loved baby Jesus, and took care of him. Jesus loved her, and he loves her still.”
Say: “When Jesus was dying on the cross, he said to his friend John, ‘Here is your mother.’ He gave Mary to all of us. Mary is our mother too. She wants us to love Jesus. She helps us.”
ask: What did Mary say to God? (Yes.)
Who is Mary? (The mother of Jesus. And our mother too.)
What do you say to your mom when she asks you to help? (Listen. Say: “Mary said yes to God. We can say yes too.”)
practice: Teach the Hail Mary’s first line, in short pieces, children repeating: “Hail Mary,” “full of grace,” “the Lord is with thee.”
Say it three times, slowly, with hands folded.
Give each child paper and crayons. Say: “Draw Mary holding baby Jesus.”
Let children show their pictures and say, “This is Mary, and this is Jesus.”
script.close: Say the first line of the Hail Mary once more. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say Hail Mary tonight with someone you love.”

tryit: Listen to how Mary said yes.
Say the first part of the Hail Mary.
Draw Mary and baby Jesus.
lessons.saintStory:
Juan Diego was an indigenous man who lived near Mexico City about five hundred years ago. One cold morning in December 1531 he was walking to Mass when he heard beautiful singing on a hill called Tepeyac.
A lady, shining like the sun, spoke to him in his own language. She said she was Mary, the mother of Jesus, and she asked him to tell the bishop to build a church there. The bishop did not believe him at first. Juan Diego carried a bundle of roses in his tilma, a cloak, to show him. When he opened it, the roses fell out, and a beautiful picture of Mary was on the cloth.
Juan Diego said yes when Mary asked for his help, and that is what Mary did when God asked her. That picture, Our Lady of Guadalupe, is still in Mexico today.

lessons.title: The saints are God’s friends
lessons.idea: Saints are people who loved God very much. Now they are with God in heaven. They pray for us.
lessons.question: Who is your favorite saint?
lessons.activity: Show pictures of three saints. Match each saint to a fact about them.
teach: Aim: holiness is for ordinary people, even children. Saints are friends who show us how to love God and who help us now, so being good feels possible, not far away.
The Church canonizes people who lived heroic virtue (CCC 828), and those in heaven keep interceding for us (CCC 956). Asking a saint to pray for us is like asking a friend, not replacing Christ.
Say: “Saints loved Jesus very much, and now they are with God and pray for us.” If asked “Where are they?”: “With God in heaven, where there is joy and no sadness.”
Avoid presenting saints as perfect from birth or only as martyrs; skip gory details. Some children may be frightened by talk of death. Pick a gentle saint such as Francis, Thérèse or a child saint.
Ask: “Who is a saint you know? What did that saint do for God?” Listen for any specific act of love. Notice whether children can say that saints once were children too.
talk: Which saint is your favorite?
What can we do to be like the saints?
Why does Jesus want us to be friends with the saints?
quiz: Saints are…|Only old people|Strangers|God’s friends|Make-believe|2|Saints love God and are with him.
Saints pray for…|Nobody|Us|Only kings|Only priests|1|Hebrews 12:1.

Which child is acting like a saint?|One who loves God and helps others|One who gets the most attention|One who wins all the games at recess|One who is never sad or tired at all|0|Saints are people who loved God very much.
Where are the saints now?|Only in statues and pictures|Gone and forgotten by God|Sleeping until the end of time|With God in heaven|3|Saints are with God in heaven.

Leo asks Saint Francis to pray for him. Is that okay?|Yes, saints pray for us|No, because saints cannot hear anything|Yes, but only on the saint’s feast day|No, only people living on earth can pray|0|The saints pray for us.
lessons.life: Choose a saint for the year and put a picture where your family can see it.
lessons.saint: Nicholas: a kind bishop who gave gifts secretly to people in need.
lessons.mem: Saint (name), pray for us.
lessons.hook: Show photos of someone’s friend, then a picture of a saint. “Saints are God’s friends.”
lessons.assess: Ask each child to name a saint or one thing a saint did.

script.open: Hold up a photo album or a framed family photo and say, “Look at my friends and family. I love them, and I think about them. God has friends, too. We call them saints.”
teach: Say: “A saint is a person who loved God very much. Some saints lived a long time ago, and some lived just a few years ago. Some were kings and some were kids, some were rich and some were poor. But they all loved Jesus most of all.”

Say: “Where are the saints now? They are in heaven with God. They are very happy. And here is a wonderful secret: the saints pray for us. When we say, ‘Saint Nicholas, pray for us,’ Saint Nicholas talks to God about us. It is like asking a good friend to put in a good word.”
Say: “You can be a saint too! God made you to be with him in heaven someday. Every day you can try to love God and be kind.”
ask: What is a saint? (A person who loved God a lot and is in heaven.)
What do the saints do for us? (They pray for us.)
Do you know the name of a saint? (Many will say their own names. Say: “Maybe you have a patron saint!”)
practice: Show pictures of three saints (Nicholas, Francis, Thérèse or ones the children know) and give one simple fact about each.
Lay out three fact cards face down: “gave gifts secretly,” “loved animals,” “loved God like a little child.”
Ask a child to turn over a card, read it with your help, and match it to a saint’s picture.
Say together after each match: “Saint ____, pray for us.”
script.close: Say the Guardian Angel prayer’s first line, or “Saint ____, pray for us” for each saint. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask your family to tell you about your name saint.”

tryit: Look at the pictures of saints.
Match each saint with a fact.
Say, “Saint ___, pray for us.”
lessons.saintStory:
Nicholas lived in the town of Myra, in what is now Turkey, about 1,700 years ago. He grew up to be a bishop, a leader of the Church, and he loved to help the poor.
A story told about him is that there was a poor man with three daughters who could not afford a gift to help them marry. In the night, Nicholas secretly tossed a bag of gold through the window. The family was able to be happy. Nicholas did not want anyone to know it was him. He gave in secret, so that only God would see.
Over the years people told this story, and Nicholas became “Santa Claus.” He was one of the saints, a friend of God, who loved to give gifts in secret.

lessons.title: Angels help us
lessons.idea: Angels are God’s helpers. Each one of us has a guardian angel who watches over us.
lessons.question: When can you say thank you to your angel?
lessons.activity: Learn the Guardian Angel prayer with hand motions.
teach: Aim: the child feels safe and not alone because God sends a helper. This is a source of comfort at bedtime and in worries, as long as it stays rooted in God’s care.
Angels are spiritual beings without bodies, God’s servants and messengers (CCC 328). Each believer has an angel as protector and guide from infancy to death (CCC 336).
Say: “Your angel is God’s helper who watches over you and prays to God for you.” If asked “Can I see my angel?”: “Usually not, because angels are spirits, but they are real.”
Do not use the angel as a threat (“your angel is watching you do wrong”); that turns comfort into fear. Skip cherub imagery; angels are not dead people and are not babies with wings.
Ask: “Who sends the angels to help us? What can we say to our angel?” See if children can say a short “Angel of God” line or name God as the one who sent the angel.
talk: How could an angel help you?
When can we say thank you to our angels?
How is an angel like a helper at home?
quiz: Who is with us all the time to help?|A king|A monster|A cartoon|A guardian angel|3|CCC 336.
Angels serve…|Only kings|Pets|God|Nobody|2|Psalm 91:11.

It is dark and Ben feels scared. What can he remember?|Angels only visit in the daytime|Angels cannot help with being scared|His guardian angel is with him|He must be brave all alone|2|Each of us has a guardian angel.
What are angels like?|God’s helpers without bodies|Babies with little wings and a bow|Statues that stay in the church|People who died and came back again|0|Angels are spirits who serve God.
Who gave you your guardian angel?|You, when you were baptized|God|The saints who live in heaven|Your parents at bedtime one night|1|God gives each of us an angel.
lessons.life: Say the guardian angel prayer at bedtime this week.
lessons.saint: Padre Pio: he said, “Our guardian angel is always with us,” and asked people to send their angel.
misc: “My angel will get angry at me.”
lessons.mem: Angel of God, my guardian dear, to whom God’s love commits me here.
lessons.hook: Whisper, “Someone is always watching over you.” Reveal an angel picture.
lessons.assess: Ask children to say the first line of the prayer with you.

script.open: Have a grown-up helper stand behind the group quietly, out of sight. Say, “I feel like someone is looking after you. Do you feel someone is here?” Reveal the helper with a smile. Say, “God has given each of you someone who is always looking after you, even when you cannot see him.”
teach: Say: “God made angels before he made us. Angels are God’s helpers. They have no bodies like we do. They love God and listen to him. They bring God’s messages. Remember the angel Gabriel who came to Mary?”
Say: “God has given each of us a special angel, who stays with us always. We call him a guardian angel. He guards us. He does not go away. When we are scared or sad, we can ask him for help.”
Say: “Jesus said that the children’s angels always see the face of the Father in heaven. So every child is very, very precious.”
ask: Who are the angels? (God’s helpers.)
Who does God give to each of us? (A guardian angel.)
When can we ask our angel for help? (When we are scared, when we are going to bed, when we are far from home.)
practice: Teach the Guardian Angel prayer a line at a time with motions: Angel of God (arms up like wings), my guardian dear (hand on heart), to whom God’s love commits me here (point up, then to yourself), ever this day (circle arm like the sun), be at my side (hand at side), to light and guard (hold hands like a candle), to rule and guide (hold hands out like a guide). Amen.
Say it twice with motions, then once while quiet.
Pair up children and let each pair say it to each other.
script.close: Say the prayer once more. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say the Guardian Angel prayer at bedtime tonight.”

tryit: Learn the Guardian Angel prayer.
Do the hand motions.
Say it quietly with a friend.
lessons.saintStory:
Francesco Forgione was born in southern Italy in 1887. As a boy he was quiet and loved to pray. At fifteen he joined the Capuchin friars and took the name Pio.
Padre Pio was a priest for many years in the little town of San Giovanni Rotondo. Long lines of people came to confession to him and to ask him to pray for them. He spent many hours in the confessional, and he said Mass with deep love. He suffered a lot, and people believed he carried the wounds of Jesus on his hands and feet.
People say Padre Pio often told those who wrote to him that he would send their guardian angel to help. His life reminds us that God gives every one of us an angel.

lessons.title: We belong to God’s family
lessons.idea: The Church is God’s family. We are baptized and belong to it. Our priest and our parish help us follow Jesus.
lessons.question: Who is in your family at church?
lessons.activity: Take a short walk around the church or look at photos. Name the people who help.
teach: Aim: each child knows “I belong to God’s family, the Church.” Belonging comes before understanding, and it supports faith better than rules in the early years.
The Church is the people called together by God (CCC 751), and Baptism makes us members of Christ’s Body and the one People of God (CCC 1267). The Church is people, not only a building.

Say: “The Church is God’s family. We belong because we are baptized.” If asked “Am I in the family if I’m not baptized?”: “God loves you always, and we welcome you, and Baptism is how a person joins God’s family.”
Children may be unbaptized, come from mixed-faith homes or family members who no longer attend. Never say who is “in” or “out.” Welcome every child warmly, and speak of others with respect.
Ask: “Who is in God’s family? Name someone in our parish.” Look for a child who names a priest, a friend, or says “all of us.” Notice whether they say “we” rather than “they.”
talk: Who is in your church family?
Who helps us at church?
Why do we call it God’s family?
quiz: The Church is…|A game|A shop|God’s family|A zoo|2|CCC 751.
We join God’s family by…|Buying|Wishing|Baptism|Winning|2|CCC 1213.

Who belongs to God’s family, the Church?|Only the priest and his helpers|Everyone who is baptized|Only people from our own parish|Only grown-ups who never sin|1|All baptized people belong to the Church.

Who helps us follow Jesus in the Church?|Only the oldest people we know|Only the people we see on TV|Our priest, parish and parents|Nobody, because we do it alone|2|The Church family helps us follow Jesus.

A new baby is baptized. What happens to her?|She joins God’s family|She stops being a little baby|She gets to start a new school|She becomes a priest someday soon|0|Baptism welcomes us into God’s family.
lessons.life: Greet someone at church by name this week.
lessons.saint: Mother Teresa: she cared for people everyone else forgot, as a mother cares for her family.
lessons.mem: We are God’s family.
lessons.hook: Hold up a family photo. “This is my family. God has a family too: the Church.”
lessons.assess: Ask: “Who is in God’s family?” (Everyone who is baptized).

script.open: Show a large paper family tree or a family photo. Ask, “Who is in this family?” Then say, “We belong to another family, too. It is bigger than any family you know. It is called the Church.”
teach: Say: “On the day you were baptized, God made you part of his family. The Church is God’s family. In this family, God is our Father, and we are all brothers and sisters.”

Say: “Who helps in our family, the Church? Father, our priest, who says Mass and forgives sins. Deacons and sisters. The people who teach you, sing, take up the collection, clean the church and welcome people at the door. And you!”

Say: “The first Christians in Jerusalem were a family. They prayed together, shared what they had and broke bread together (Acts 2). We do those things too: we pray together, we share, and we go to Mass.”
ask: Who is in God’s family? (Everyone who is baptized.)
Who is the priest at our parish? (Say his name together.)
How can you help our parish family? (Welcome someone, share, be quiet at Mass, pray for others.)
practice: Take a short walk around the church or parish building, or look at photos of the people who work there.
At each stop say the person’s name and what they do: “This is Father ___. He says Mass.”
Let children give a wave or a thank-you.
Sit and say together: “Thank you, God, for our family, the Church.”
script.close: Hold hands in a circle. Say: “We are God’s family.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family one person who helps at church.”

tryit: Look at the people who help at our parish.
Say each person’s name.
Thank them in a prayer.
lessons.saintStory:
Agnes Gonxha was born in 1910 in what is now North Macedonia. When she grew up she became a nun and took the name Teresa. She went to India to teach, and then one day she heard Jesus calling her to serve the poorest people.
In the city of Calcutta she began to take care of people who were sick, hungry and dying, and who were lying in the streets. She started a family of sisters, the Missionaries of Charity, who cared for them with love. Many people joined her, and houses opened all over the world.
Mother Teresa died in 1997 and was named a saint in 2016. She said the poor are Jesus in disguise. The Church is a family that takes care of everyone, just as she did.

lessons.title: Our church building
lessons.idea: The church is God’s house. We are quiet and respectful there because Jesus is present. We find the altar, the cross and the tabernacle.
lessons.question: What helps us be quiet in church?
lessons.activity: Practice making the Sign of the Cross with holy water, genuflecting and sitting quietly.
teach: Aim: the child learns that church is a special place because Jesus is present there, so we act with quiet respect and joy. Reverence is learned by doing, at this age.
The church building is a place for the assembled people to worship (CCC 1179), and the tabernacle holds the Blessed Sacrament for adoration, where Jesus is really present (CCC 1183).
Say: “This is God’s house, and Jesus is truly here in the tabernacle. We use quiet voices, because we are with him.” If asked “Is he really in there?”: “Yes. We believe it because Jesus promised.”

Avoid making quietness a punishment or demanding stillness beyond a five-year-old’s ability. Some children are used to noisy worship or none at all. Teach the walk and the bow as a way to greet a friend.
Take a short walk through the church and ask each child to point to the altar, cross and tabernacle. See who whispers and who genuflects or bows without being told.
talk: What do you see in our church?
Why do we make the Sign of the Cross?
How do we show respect for Jesus?
quiz: Where is Jesus kept in church?|In the tabernacle|At home|In a book|In the car|0|CCC 1379.
Holy water reminds us of…|A swimming pool|Our Baptism|Rain|A drink|1|CCC 1668.
Why are we quiet and careful in church?|It is a game to see who talks|The room is easily broken by noise|Jesus is truly there|The priest likes silence the best|2|Jesus is present in the tabernacle.
Where is Jesus kept in the church?|In the tabernacle|Behind the front doors of the church|By the holy water near the door|Under the pews where we sit|0|Jesus is truly there in the tabernacle.

Ben runs and shouts in church. What is the better choice?|Keep running but whisper while he does|Shout only when no one is looking|Hide so no one notices him|Walk quietly; it is God’s house|3|We show respect for God’s house.
lessons.life: Visit the church with a grown-up and look for the cross, the altar and the tabernacle.
lessons.saint: Tarcisius: a boy who carried Jesus in the Eucharist and protected him.
lessons.mem: I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the Lord.” (Psalm 122:1)
lessons.hook: Walk into the church quietly with the children. Whisper, “This is God’s house.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to point to the altar and tabernacle.

script.open: Put a cloth over something very special (a framed photo of the tabernacle, or a small gold box). Say very softly, “I have something very special. We must be very quiet and careful with it.” Lift the cloth slowly. “This is where Jesus lives in our church.”
teach: Say: “A church is not like other buildings. It is God’s house. Jesus is truly there, in the tabernacle. That is why we are quiet, and why we are gentle.”

Point out, with pictures or in the real church: the altar (where Mass is said), the cross (to remember that Jesus died for us), the tabernacle with its little red light (it shows that Jesus is there), and the holy water (to remember our Baptism).

Say: “When we come in, we dip our fingers in holy water and make the Sign of the Cross. When we pass the tabernacle, we genuflect, which means we touch one knee to the floor to say hello to Jesus. In the pew we sit, stand and kneel quietly.”
ask: Whose house is the church? (God’s.)
How do we act in God’s house? (Quietly, kindly, gently.)
What does the red light by the tabernacle mean? (Jesus is here.)
practice: If you can, go into the church. If not, make an “aisle” with tape on the floor and a pretend tabernacle at the end.
Teach three actions: dip fingers and make the Sign of the Cross, genuflect, and sit with hands folded.
Let each child walk the aisle slowly, one at a time, while the others watch and say “Welcome, Jesus.”
Finish by sitting very quietly for twenty seconds.
script.close: Say: “Jesus, we are glad to be in your house.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Next Sunday, show your family how to genuflect.”

tryit: Walk quietly into the church.
Make the Sign of the Cross and genuflect.
Sit still and listen.
lessons.saintStory:
Tarcisius lived in Rome about 1,700 years ago, in a time when it was dangerous to be a Christian. He was a young boy who served at Mass.
One day the priest needed someone to carry the Eucharist to Christians who were in prison, so they could receive Jesus. Tarcisius said he would do it. He held the Eucharist close to his chest and walked through the streets. Some bullies stopped him and asked what he was carrying. He would not show them, and he would not let them take Jesus.
Tarcisius died protecting the Eucharist. He shows us how much to respect Jesus in the church, and why we are quiet and careful there.

lessons.title: We go to Mass on Sunday
lessons.idea: On Sunday we go to Mass. We sing, listen, pray and thank God. It is the day of Jesus’ Resurrection.
lessons.question: Who do you go to church with?
lessons.activity: Make a “Sunday basket” of items you see at Mass. Name each one.
teach: Aim: the child learns Sunday is special because Jesus rose on that day, and that Mass is where God’s family meets him. Joy matters more than obligation at this age.
Sunday is the Lord’s Day, the day of the Resurrection and the new creation (CCC 2174). The Sunday Eucharist is at the heart of the Church’s life (CCC 2177).
Say: “On Sunday we go to Mass to thank Jesus, who rose from the dead.” If asked “Why must we go?”: “Because Jesus invites his family to come, and it’s the best way to thank him.”
Do not shame children for missing Mass; they rarely choose it. Some have parents who work Sundays or do not attend. Celebrate the Sunday they do come, and invite families without pressure.
Ask: “What day is Mass? What do we do there?” Look for answers like sing, pray, listen or thank. Notice whether any child mentions Jesus rising.
talk: What do you like about Mass?
What do we do when we gather?
How do we get ready for Sunday?
quiz: On Sunday, Christians go to…|The mall|A race|Mass|Work|2|CCC 2177.
Sunday celebrates…|Nothing|A holiday for toys|A birthday|The day Jesus rose|3|CCC 1166.

Why do Christians go to Mass on Sunday?|It is the day Jesus rose|It is the day we rest from school|It is the day for wearing good clothes|It is the first day we clean the house|0|Sunday is the day of Jesus’ Resurrection.

What do we do at Mass?|Sit silently and only watch the priest|Visit and talk with our friends|Practice for a big performance|Sing, listen, pray and thank God|3|At Mass we sing, listen, pray and thank God.
A friend missed Mass. What should we do?|Invite him and welcome him|Say that he cannot belong anymore|Tell him he is in big trouble|Ignore him from now on|0|We invite and welcome; we do not shame.
lessons.life: Lay out your “Mass clothes” on Saturday night with your family.
lessons.saint: Bl. Imelda: a girl who loved Jesus in the Eucharist so much that she longed to receive him.
lessons.mem: This is the day the Lord has made. (Psalm 118:24)
lessons.hook: Ring a bell. Say, “It’s Sunday! What do you do on Sunday?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What do we do at Mass?”

script.open: Come in with a basket covered by a cloth. Say, “I have a Sunday basket. It has things we see and use at Mass. Can anyone guess what is inside?” Take out one item at a time (a small cross, a candle, a children’s Mass book, a coin for the collection, a missal ribbon) and ask what it is.
teach: Say: “Sunday is a special day. On the first Easter Sunday, Jesus rose from the dead. That is why Christians gather every Sunday, to say thank you and to celebrate Jesus. The psalm says: ‘This is the day the Lord has made. Let us rejoice and be glad.’”
Say: “At Mass we do many things. We sing. We listen to God’s word. We pray. We bring gifts. And then Jesus comes to us in Holy Communion. We say thank you to God.”
Say: “Going to Mass is not like going to a show. It is like coming to a family dinner. Jesus invites us, and he is the host.”
ask: What day do we go to Mass? (Sunday.)
What do we do at Mass? (Sing, pray, listen, thank God.)
Why do we call Sunday a special day? (Jesus rose on a Sunday.)
practice: Pass around each item in the basket. Say its name and what it is for.
Let the children put each item in a shoebox “Sunday basket” while you say, “At Mass we use a ___.”
Teach one simple response, such as “Thanks be to God.” Practice it three times.
Close the basket and say: “On Sunday, God is waiting for us.”
script.close: Say: “This is the day the Lord has made.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “On Sunday, look for one thing from our basket at Mass.”

tryit: Look at the things we see at Mass.
Say the name of each one.
Put them in the Sunday basket.
lessons.saintStory:
Imelda Lambertini was born in Bologna, Italy, in 1322. She was a girl who loved Jesus very much, and her parents sent her to live with Dominican sisters when she was nine. She loved to pray in front of the tabernacle.
In those days children usually received First Communion when they were older, and Imelda longed to receive Jesus. She wished with all her heart that she could. On the day of Ascension, in 1333, when she was eleven, a priest gave her Holy Communion. She was filled with joy. She died soon after, still smiling, right after receiving Jesus.
Imelda is the patron saint of First Communicants. She helps us see how wonderful Sunday Mass is, when we get to be near Jesus.

lessons.title: Baptism makes us God’s children
lessons.idea: In Baptism, water is poured and God’s family welcomes us. We get a white garment and a candle. God’s life is in us.
lessons.question: What happens at a baptism?
lessons.activity: Look at a baptism candle. Each child blows out and re-lights a safe LED candle and says, “Jesus is my light.”
teach: Aim: the child understands that in Baptism God made them his own child and part of his family. Identity as a beloved child of God is the root of Christian life.

Baptism is the gateway to life in the Spirit and frees us from sin, making us children of God and members of Christ (CCC 1213). The white garment and candle show we belong to Christ the light (CCC 1243, 1262).
Say: “When you were baptized, water was poured and God made you his child.” If asked “What if I wasn’t baptized?”: “God loves you very much. Ask your parents about Baptism; the Church welcomes you.”
Some children are not baptized, or Baptism was in another church. Do not imply they are less loved. Never use “saved” or “unsaved” language. Invite parents privately to speak with the priest.
Show a candle, water and white cloth and ask what each means. Look for “God’s child”, “light” and “family.” Ask who has a baptism day to share.
talk: Do you know your baptism day?
What did they give you? (A white garment, a candle.)
Who are your godparents?
quiz: In Baptism we get…|A car|A cake|A new toy|Water and God’s life|3|CCC 1214-1216.
Baptism makes us…|Kings|Strangers|Soldiers|God’s children|3|CCC 1265.
What does the white garment at Baptism show?|New life with God|That we are in a school play|That we are rich and fancy now|That we will never get dirty|0|The garment shows our new life in God.

What does the baptismal candle remind us of?|That churches need to be well lit|That it is a birthday for babies|Jesus is our light|That we should keep matches safe|2|The candle shows we carry Jesus’ light.

Baby Rosa is baptized today. What is now true?|She is God’s child in the Church|She is now a grown-up helper|She can receive the Eucharist now|She will never do anything wrong|0|Baptism makes us God’s children.
lessons.life: Ask your parents to tell the story of your baptism day. Look at the photos.
lessons.saint: Lucy: a girl who stayed faithful to Christ; her name means light, like the baptismal candle.
lessons.mem: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
lessons.hook: Pour a little water into a bowl and let children touch it. “Water gives life and cleans.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to show the Sign of the Cross.

script.open: Dim the lights and put a baptism candle (or an LED candle) in the middle of the circle. Say, “Everyone, watch the candle. What does the light do?” Turn it on. “It makes the dark go away. A very special candle was lit for you on the day of your Baptism.”
teach: Say: “When you were a baby, your family took you to church. The priest poured water on your head, and said, ‘I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’ And you became a child of God. God’s own life came into you. That is called grace.”

Say: “You were wrapped in a white garment, to show that you were clean and new. And a candle was lit from the big Easter candle. The priest said, ‘Receive the light of Christ.’ That candle means: Jesus is our light, and we should shine too.”

Say: “Jesus told his friends to baptize everyone: ‘Go and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’ That is what we say when we make the Sign of the Cross. It reminds us of Baptism.”
ask: What happens at Baptism? (Water, words, God’s family, God’s life.)
What do you see in the candle? (Light. Jesus is our light.)
What words are said at Baptism? (In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.)
practice: Show a real baptism candle if possible, or the photo of the child’s own baptism.
Give each child an LED candle. Say: “This is not a real flame, so it is safe.”
Say, as you turn on the light: “Jesus is my light.” Then switch it off and say, “I can shine for Jesus.”
Turn it on again together.
Let children shine their candles for each other and say, “You are a child of God.”
script.close: Hold the candles up and say: “Thank you, God, for making us your children.” Make the Sign of the Cross slowly. Send home: “Ask to see your baptism photo, candle or gown.”

tryit: Look at a baptism candle.
Light the LED candle and say: “Jesus is my light.”
Blow it out, then light it again.
lessons.saintStory:
Lucy lived on the island of Sicily about 1,700 years ago, when it was dangerous to be a Christian. Her name means “light.”
She belonged to a rich family, but she gave away her goods to help the poor. She would not give up her faith in Jesus, even when she was told that she must. She stayed faithful until she died. People tell that she brought food to Christians who were hiding underground and wore a crown of candles on her head to light the way, so her hands were free to carry food.
Lucy’s feast day, December 13, is celebrated with lights. At Baptism we receive a candle that is lit from the Easter candle. It says that Christ is our light, as he was for Lucy.

lessons.title: The Eucharist is Jesus’ gift
lessons.idea: At Mass, bread and wine become Jesus. He gives himself to us. We prepare our hearts to receive him someday.
lessons.question: Why do we kneel at the consecration?
lessons.activity: Practice reverent hands and reverent posture. Draw an altar with a chalice.
teach: Aim: the child learns that at Mass Jesus gives himself to us and that we love and respect him in this gift. Reverence grows from knowing who Jesus is, not from fear.

At the Last Supper Jesus gave us the Eucharist (CCC 1323), and after the consecration his Body and Blood, soul and divinity are truly, really and substantially present under the appearances of bread and wine (CCC 1374).
Say: “At Mass the bread and wine become Jesus, though they still look the same. He gives himself to us.” If asked “Is it a symbol?”: “It is a sign, and also really Jesus. That’s what Jesus said.”
Do not make children feel excluded if they do not yet receive; invite a spiritual communion. Avoid tasting games or ordinary-food comparisons, and never joke about the host.
Ask: “Who is in the tabernacle? What does the priest say?” Watch how they hold their hands and bow. See if any say “Jesus” without being prompted.
talk: How do we show love for Jesus at Mass?
What can you say to Jesus in your heart?
Why do we kneel?
quiz: At Mass, bread and wine become…|Water|A symbol only|Candy|Jesus|3|CCC 1376.
We show respect by…|Playing|Running|Being quiet and kind|Shouting|2|Reverence.

Why is Communion different from a snack?|It is a prize for good kids|It is only a reminder of him|Bread and wine become Jesus|It is a bigger piece of bread|2|At Mass bread and wine become Jesus’ Body and Blood.
How can we get ready to receive Jesus?|Rush up to the front of the line|Prepare our hearts|Chat with the friends beside us|Check who is watching us|1|We prepare our hearts to receive Jesus.

Lena is too young to receive Communion yet. What can she do?|Pray, “Jesus, I love you, come into my heart”|Wait outside while the others pray|Skip Mass until she is older|Ask for a bite of her friend’s bread|0|She can make a spiritual communion.
lessons.life: Make a quiet “thank you, Jesus” card to place in your Bible or prayer corner.
lessons.saint: Pius X: the pope who invited children to receive Jesus in Holy Communion.
misc: “I am left out because I can’t receive.”
lessons.mem: Jesus, I love you. Come into my heart.
lessons.hook: Hold bread gently. “Bread helps us grow strong. At Mass, bread becomes Jesus.”
lessons.assess: Ask: “Who is in the Eucharist?” (Jesus).

script.open: Show a loaf of bread and a cup of grape juice. Say, “What are these? Bread and juice. We eat them for lunch. But at Mass, something amazing happens to bread and wine. Let me tell you.”
teach: Say: “The night before Jesus died, he ate a meal with his friends, called the Last Supper. He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and said, ‘Take this, all of you, and eat it. This is my body.’ Then he took the cup and said, ‘This is my blood.’ And he said, ‘Do this in memory of me.’” (Luke 22:19)

Say: “The priest does what Jesus did, at every Mass. He says Jesus’ own words, and the bread and wine become Jesus. They still look the same, but they are really Jesus. That is a big mystery. We call it the Eucharist.”

Say: “Jesus gives himself to us. When the children are older, they can receive Jesus in Holy Communion. Now we are getting our hearts ready. How? We learn about Jesus, we pray, we say sorry when we do something wrong, and we are kind.”
ask: What happens to the bread and wine at Mass? (They become Jesus.)
Why does Jesus give himself to us? (Because he loves us.)
How can we get ready to receive Jesus? (Pray, be kind, say sorry.)
practice: Show how to hold hands as a throne (left over right, palms up) and fold hands to show respect.
Practice walking slowly, hands folded, to the front of the room and back.
Give paper and crayons. Say: “Draw an altar with a cup, a chalice.”
As children draw, say the prayer softly: “Jesus, I love you. Come into my heart.”
script.close: Say the prayer together: “Jesus, I love you. Come into my heart.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask when you can see the tabernacle at church.”

tryit: Show reverent hands.
Practice walking and kneeling reverently.
Draw an altar with a chalice.
lessons.saintStory:
Giuseppe Sarto was born in 1835 in the small Italian village of Riese, into a poor family. As a boy he walked several miles to school each day, and he carried his shoes in his hand to save them for church. He became a priest, then a bishop, and in 1903 he became pope and took the name Pius X.
Pope Pius X loved the Eucharist very much, and he wanted everyone to receive Jesus often. In 1910 he said that children could make their First Communion when they were about seven years old, as soon as they could understand that the bread is Jesus. Before that, many children had to wait until they were much older.
Because of Pius X, children all over the world can receive Jesus early. His life shows that Jesus is a gift for the young, and that we should get our hearts ready.

lessons.title: God forgives
lessons.idea: When we do wrong, we can say sorry. God is always ready to forgive. He loves us even when we make mistakes.
lessons.question: What do we say when we are sorry?
lessons.activity: Role-play “I’m sorry. I forgive you.” Read a picture book about forgiveness.
teach: Aim: a child knows that mistakes are not the end, and that God forgives when we are sorry. This prevents a hidden fear that God’s love must be earned.
In Penance we receive God’s mercy and are reconciled with him and the Church (CCC 1422). The parable of the merciful father shows the heart of repentance (CCC 1439).
Say: “When we do wrong, we can say sorry and God always forgives, like the father who ran to his son.” If asked “What if I do it again?”: “God still forgives. We try again, and he helps us.”
Avoid fear, guilt or lists of sins. Do not suggest God is angry or keeping score. Some children are scrupulous or punished severely at home; keep your voice calm and the focus on God’s welcome.
Role-play a small hurt: one child says sorry and another says “I forgive you.” Ask “How did God feel about the son?” and listen for “happy” or “hugged him.”
talk: What did you do when you hurt someone?
How did it feel when someone forgave you?
What does God do when we say sorry?
quiz: When we do wrong, God…|Is angry forever|Leaves|Forgets us|Is ready to forgive|3|CCC 1439.
We say…|“You’re wrong”|Nothing|“I’m sorry”|“Whatever”|2|Reconciliation.
Jada broke a toy and feels bad. What can she do?|Say sorry; God forgives|Hide it so that nobody ever knows|Hope that God did not see it|Wait until she is perfect|0|God is always ready to forgive.

Does God stop loving us when we make mistakes?|No, he loves us and forgives|Only on days when he is not busy|Yes, if the mistake is a big one|Yes, until we say sorry loudly|0|God loves us even when we make mistakes.

In Jesus’ story, the father saw his son coming home. What did he do?|He pretended not to see him|He ran to hug him|He made him stay outside the gate|He asked for the money back first|1|God is like the father who forgives.
lessons.life: This week say “I’m sorry” the moment you hurt someone.
lessons.saint: Maria Goretti: a girl who forgave as she was dying.
misc: “God is mad at me when I do wrong.”
lessons.mem: Jesus, I am sorry. Please forgive me.
lessons.hook: Tell about a child who broke a cup and hid. “How did he feel? What could he do?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What do we say when we hurt someone?”

script.open: Read a short picture book where a character says sorry. Or say, “Do you know what to do when you make a mistake? I spilled juice on a book today, and I felt so bad.” Tell the story and ask, “What should I do?”
teach: Tell the story from Luke 15 in your own words: “A man had two sons. The younger one said, ‘Father, give me my share.’ He went far away and spent all his money. Then he had nothing to eat. He said, ‘I will go back and say, I am sorry.’ And while he was still far away, his father saw him, ran to him, hugged him and kissed him. The father said, ‘Let’s have a party! My son was lost, and now he’s found.’”
Say: “The father in the story is like God. When we do something wrong, God is not angry forever. When we say sorry, he runs to us. He hugs us and forgives us. God’s love is bigger than our mistakes.”
Say: “When we do something wrong, we feel sad inside. We can tell God, ‘I am sorry.’ And God forgives. Later we will learn about a sacrament called Reconciliation, where a priest helps us.”
ask: What did the son do wrong? (He took the money and spent it, and left.)
What did the father do when the son came back? (He ran, hugged and forgave him.)
What can we say to God when we do something wrong? (I’m sorry.)
practice: Choose a simple pretend situation: “Someone knocks down your tower.”
Show two children how to say “I’m sorry” and “I forgive you,” with a hug or handshake.
Let each pair practice. Walk around and help.
Come back together and say as a group: “Jesus, I am sorry. Please forgive me.”
script.close: Sign of the Cross. Say: “Thank you, God, for forgiving us.” Send home: “Say sorry to someone this week, and forgive someone too.”

tryit: Listen to the story of the lost son.
Practice: “I’m sorry. I forgive you.”
Hug your partner.
lessons.saintStory:
Maria Goretti was born in Italy in 1890 to a poor farming family. When her father died, her mother worked hard to feed the children, and Maria helped by cooking, cleaning and caring for her little brothers and sisters.
She was a gentle, prayerful girl, and she was looking forward to making her First Communion. One day, when she was eleven, a young man named Alessandro, who lived near her, did a terrible thing to her. She was hurt so badly that she died the next day. Before she died, Maria forgave him and said she wanted him in heaven with her.
Alessandro was in prison for many years and was very sorry. He asked for forgiveness from Maria’s mother, who forgave him. Maria shows how strong forgiveness is, and that God always forgives when we are sorry.

units.title: Loving others
units.eq: How does Jesus want us to love?

lessons.title: Love God and love others
lessons.idea: Jesus said to love God and love our neighbor. We show love by being kind, sharing and helping.
lessons.question: How can you show love at home?
lessons.activity: Make a “kindness chain”: add a paper link for each kind act this week.
teach: Aim: the child sees that following Jesus means loving God and loving others in small daily actions. Love is a habit practiced at snack time and on the playground.
Jesus summed up the Law in two commands: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself (Mark 12:29–31; CCC 2055, 2196). Love of neighbor flows from love of God.
Say: “Love God first, and show it by being kind to others.” If asked “Do I have to love everyone?”: “We try to be kind to everyone. Loving means wanting good for them, even when it’s hard.”
Do not promise that kindness always feels easy, or teach children to ignore being hurt. A child can be kind and still tell a grown-up if someone is unkind. Avoid ranking kids by how nice they are.
Watch the day for a real moment of sharing or helping and name it: “You loved your neighbor.” Ask children to say one way to love God and one way to love a friend.
talk: How do you like to be treated?
What is one kind thing you did today?
Who needs a friend at school?
quiz: The Golden Rule says…|Hide|Win|Treat others as you want to be treated|Be first|2|Matthew 7:12.
Jesus wants us to love…|Only family|Only ourselves|God and our neighbor|Only friends|2|Mark 12:30-31.

A new girl sits alone at lunch. What is the loving thing?|Tell her where an empty seat is|Leave her so she can think by herself|Invite her to sit with you|Wait for a grown-up to help her|2|We show love by being kind and including others.
Which choice shows love for your neighbor?|Keeping the best ones for later|Sharing your crayons|Giving only to your best friend|Lending them if you get paid|1|Sharing is a way we love others.
How can we show love for God?|By loving other people|By having the very nicest toys|By knowing every Bible story|By being very quiet all day long|0|Jesus said to love God and love our neighbor.
lessons.life: Do one kind thing a day this week; draw a heart each time.
lessons.saint: Martin de Porres: a Peruvian friar who loved the poor and animals.
lessons.mem: Love one another. (John 13:34)
lessons.hook: Hold a paper heart. “Jesus said the most important rule is love.”
lessons.assess: Ask each child to name one kind thing they will do.

script.open: Hold up a heart cut from paper. Say, “Jesus told us the two most important things in the whole world. They both have the word ‘love’ in them. Can you guess what they are?” Let children guess, then say: “Love God, and love other people.”
teach: Say: “One day someone asked Jesus, ‘What is the most important thing God wants us to do?’ Jesus said, ‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart. And love your neighbor as yourself.’ (Mark 12:29-31)”

Say: “We love God when we pray, say thank you, go to Mass and listen to him. We love others when we share, take turns, help, include a lonely child, and use kind words. Whenever we do something kind for someone, we are loving Jesus, too.”
Say: “Love is not just a feeling. Love is something we do. A kind act is a way of saying, ‘I love you.’”
ask: What are the two most important things? (Love God. Love others.)
How can we show love to someone at school? (Share, play together, help.)
What is one kind thing you did this week? (Let several share.)
practice: Cut strips of colored paper.
Say: “Think of one kind thing you can do this week.” Help each child tell you or draw it on a strip.
Make a loop with each strip and link them into a chain, one link at a time.
Hang the chain on the wall. Add a link each time a child does something kind.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, help us love you and love each other.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one kind thing every day and tell us about it.”

tryit: Think of a kind thing you can do.
Write or draw it on a paper link.
Add your link to the chain.
lessons.saintStory:
Martin de Porres was born in Lima, Peru, in 1579. His father was a Spanish nobleman and his mother was a freed woman from Panama, and some people were unkind to him because of the color of his skin.
Martin became a Dominican brother, and the sisters and brothers soon discovered how much he cared for people. He worked in the infirmary, caring for the sick, whether they were rich or poor, and he gave his food to those who were hungry. He also loved animals, and it is said that a dog, a cat and a mouse ate from the same dish at his feet.
Martin shows us how to love God and love others: be kind, share, and help, no matter who people are.

lessons.title: Telling the truth
lessons.idea: God wants us to tell the truth. Lies hurt people. Telling the truth makes us feel free.
lessons.question: How does it feel when someone tells you the truth?
lessons.activity: Read a story where a character is honest. Act it out with puppets.
