teach: Aim: the child learns truth is safe and good, and that honesty keeps friendships trusting. Five-year-olds mix pretend and lies, so gently teach the difference.
The eighth commandment forbids misrepresenting the truth, because God is truth (CCC 2464), and truthfulness is the virtue of being true in word and deed (CCC 2468). Jesus says the truth sets us free.
Say: “God wants us to say what is true, even when it’s hard, and he helps us be brave.” If asked “Is it a lie to pretend?”: “No, play pretend is fun. A lie is trying to trick someone.”
Do not punish honesty harshly; a child who is scolded for confessing learns to hide. Fear of consequences drives lying. Be honest yourself, and thank children for owning up.
Present a small scenario (a spilled juice) and ask what to say. Look for “I did it” and “I’m sorry.” Notice who says a lie is wrong because it hurts.
talk: What does it feel like to tell the truth?
Who can you tell when you are afraid to tell the truth?
What does a lie do to a friendship?
quiz: God wants us to…|Hide things|Lie|Pretend|Tell the truth|3|Exodus 20:16.
When we tell the truth we feel…|Sick|Lost|Trapped|Free|3|John 8:32.
Noah broke a cup. What is the better choice?|Say it was already cracked|Hide the pieces away|Tell the truth about it|Say the dog did it|2|God wants us to tell the truth.
Why is telling a lie bad?|It makes the grown-ups very tired|It hurts people|It is rude to be too clever|It is hard to remember what we said|1|Lies hurt people.

After telling the truth about a mistake, how do we often feel?|Sure that we will never be caught|Free and light inside|Proud that we fooled everyone|Worried about being found out|1|Telling the truth makes us feel free.
lessons.life: Choose one day this week for “truth day”: tell the truth no matter what.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: a man who told the truth even when it cost him.
misc: “Telling the truth always gets me in trouble.”
lessons.mem: The truth will set you free. (John 8:32)
lessons.hook: Show two faces, one hiding and one open. “Which feels freer?” Read a short story about honesty.
lessons.assess: Ask: “What do we do when we have done something wrong?”

script.open: Use two hand puppets. One puppet says, “I did not break the cup!” with a very sneaky voice while holding a broken cup behind it. Ask the children: “Is the puppet telling the truth? How do you know?”
teach: Say: “God wants us to tell the truth. One of God’s ten rules says, ‘You shall not tell lies.’ (Exodus 20:16) When we tell a lie, we say something that is not true, and that hurts people, because they cannot trust us.”

Say: “Sometimes we are scared to tell the truth, because we think we will be in trouble. But Jesus said, ‘The truth will set you free.’ (John 8:32) When we tell the truth, we feel light and free, like we put down something heavy.”
Say: “Telling the truth is brave. It is okay to say, ‘I did it, and I am sorry.’ God is proud of us when we tell the truth, and the people who love us are, too.”
ask: What is a lie? (Saying something that is not true.)
Why is it hard to tell the truth sometimes? (We are scared of trouble.)
How do you feel after telling the truth? (Better, free, happy.)
practice: Read a short picture book in which a character tells the truth when it is hard (for example, about a broken vase or a missing cookie).
Give the children the two puppets. Let pairs act out: puppet 1 breaks something, puppet 2 asks what happened.
Practice the brave answer: “I did it. I’m sorry.”
Cheer for each pair.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, help us tell the truth.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell the truth this week, even if it’s hard.”

tryit: Listen to the story of honest Tom.
Act it out with a puppet.
Say: “The truth will set you free.”
lessons.saintStory:
Thomas More was an English lawyer and writer who lived about 500 years ago. He was known to be honest and wise, and the king, Henry VIII, made him an important leader of the country. He was also a loving father to his children.
When the king wanted Thomas to say something that he did not believe was true, Thomas refused. He said what he believed, even though it would cost him. The king put him in prison, and later Thomas was executed. His last words were that he was “the king’s good servant, but God’s first.”
Thomas More was named a saint. He shows us that the truth matters more than being safe, and that God helps those who tell the truth.

lessons.title: Saying sorry and forgiving
lessons.idea: When we hurt someone, we say sorry. When someone hurts us, we forgive. Jesus forgives us, so we can forgive too.
lessons.question: What can you do after you hurt a friend?
lessons.activity: Practice a sorry-and-forgive routine with a partner.
teach: Aim: the child has words to say sorry and a first understanding of forgiving. Reconciliation is learned in tiny daily hurts, and it grows from knowing Jesus forgives us first.
We ask forgiveness and forgive because God forgave us; in the Our Father we ask to be forgiven as we forgive (CCC 2843, 2842). Forgiving is a choice to be kind, not necessarily a feeling.

Say: “When we hurt someone, we say sorry. When someone hurts us, we forgive, because Jesus forgave us.” If asked “What if they hurt me again?”: “Tell a grown-up. Forgiving doesn’t mean letting it keep happening.”

Never force a child to hug or say “it’s okay” to someone who hurt them. Forgiveness is not the same as staying in unsafe situations. If a child describes being harmed, tell a trusted adult right away.
Observe a real conflict and coach: “What can you say?” Look for a clear “I’m sorry” and a returning “I forgive you,” and a child who goes back to play.
talk: When have you forgiven someone?
What do you say when you want to forgive?
Who forgives us always?
quiz: When someone says sorry, we can…|Hit|Ignore|Forgive|Tease|2|Matthew 18:21-22.
Jesus forgives us so we can…|Be mean|Keep score|Forgive others|Run away|2|Ephesians 4:32.
Mia pushed Jake by accident. What should she do?|Wait for him to say it first|Say that Jake got in her way|Run away fast so he cannot see her|Say, “I am sorry”|3|When we hurt someone we say sorry.

Jake says, “I forgive you.” What does that mean?|He will never play with her again|He is not angry and stays her friend|He will push her back later on|He does not mind being hurt at all|1|Forgiving means choosing to be kind.
Why can we forgive people who hurt us?|Nobody really means to hurt us|Grown-ups make us do it|It never hurts us in the first place|Jesus forgave us first|3|Jesus forgives us, so we can forgive too.
lessons.life: If someone upsets you this week, say “It’s okay. I forgive you.”
lessons.saint: Maria Goretti: she forgave her attacker with her last words.
misc: “If I forgive, I must play with them.”
lessons.mem: Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.
lessons.hook: Tear a paper heart and tape it. “It mends when we say sorry and forgive.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to act out “I’m sorry” and “I forgive you.”

script.open: Have two dolls or puppets: one takes the other’s toy. Say, “Oh no. Now what should happen? The first puppet is sorry. The second one is sad. What should they say?”
teach: Say: “Sometimes people hurt us, and sometimes we hurt people. Both are very hard. But Jesus shows us what to do. When we hurt someone, we say sorry. When someone hurts us, we forgive.”

Tell: “Peter once asked Jesus, ‘How many times should I forgive someone? Seven times?’ And Jesus said, ‘Not seven times, but seventy times seven.’ That means always, over and over.” (Matthew 18:21-22)
Say: “We pray this in the Our Father: ‘Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.’ Jesus forgives us, so we can forgive, too. It is not easy. But Jesus helps us.”
ask: What do we say when we hurt someone? (I’m sorry.)
What do we say when someone says sorry? (I forgive you.)
Who helps us forgive? (Jesus.)
practice: Teach the two phrases: “I’m sorry.” and “I forgive you.” Say them with actions (hand on heart, then open hands).
Pair up children. Say: “One of you pretends to bump the other. The other says, ‘That’s okay, I forgive you.’”
Let partners switch roles.
Come back and give each child a sticker of a heart, saying, “Forgiving is brave.”
script.close: Say the line from the Our Father: “Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “If someone says sorry to you, say, ‘I forgive you.’”

tryit: Say: “I’m sorry.”
Answer: “I forgive you.”
Shake hands or give a hug.
lessons.saintStory:
Maria Goretti was an Italian girl who lived about 120 years ago. Her family was poor, and Maria worked hard at home and prayed a lot.
When she was eleven, a young man named Alessandro hurt her very badly. In the hospital she was in great pain, but she said that she forgave him and that she wanted him to be with her in heaven. She died the next day.
Years later Alessandro was sorry. Maria’s forgiveness helped him change his heart, and he asked God and her family for forgiveness. Maria teaches us that forgiving is very strong, and God helps us do it.

units.title: Praying every day
units.eq: How do we talk to God?

lessons.title: We can talk to God
lessons.idea: Prayer is talking to God. We can pray with words, with songs or in quiet. God always listens.
lessons.question: When can you pray?
lessons.activity: Pray in silence for one minute, then a simple prayer: “Thank you, God. I love you.”
teach: Aim: the child learns that prayer is simply talking and listening to God, anywhere, in any words. The goal is relationship, not performance or the right formula.
Prayer is raising the mind and heart to God (CCC 2559), and in the New Covenant it is the living relationship of God’s children with their Father (CCC 2565). Jesus invites us to pray in simple trust.

Say: “Prayer is talking to God like a friend, and also being quiet with him.” If asked “Does God answer?”: “Yes, he always listens. Sometimes he answers in ways we don’t expect, and he always loves us.”

Avoid making prayer a long, still obligation. Some children have never prayed; others pray scripted prayers only. Accept short, wiggly, silly-sweet prayers. Do not promise God will give every request.
Invite a thirty-second quiet and then a spoken prayer: “Thank you, God for…” See who can talk to God in their own words and who needs a sentence to begin.
talk: What would you tell God today?
When is it easy to pray?
How do you feel when you pray?
quiz: Prayer is talking with…|The TV|The wall|A phone|God|3|CCC 2559.
We can pray…|Anywhere|Only at church|Only on Sunday|Never|0|1 Thessalonians 5:17.
Which one is a way to pray?|Being quiet and thinking of God|Only reading out loud from a book|Only praying while in church|Saying words as fast as you can|0|We can pray with words, songs or in quiet.
Emma does not know the right words for God. What is okay?|Skip praying that day|Wait until she learns many more|Talk in her own words|Let a grown-up pray for her|2|Any loving words are prayer.
Does God hear a quiet prayer in your heart?|Yes, he always listens|Only if you use the right words|Only if you say it out loud|Only if you are standing in church|0|God always listens.
lessons.life: Pick a time and place for a daily prayer with your family.
lessons.saint: Bernadette Soubirous: a girl who prayed the Rosary and saw Our Lady at Lourdes.
lessons.mem: Thank you, God. I love you.
lessons.hook: Hold a toy phone to your ear. “We can talk to God anywhere.”
lessons.assess: Ask each child to say a short prayer.

script.open: Start with a surprise: whisper, and ask the children to whisper back. “God can hear whispers. Today we’re going to talk about how to talk to God.”
teach: Say: “Prayer is talking to God, and listening to him, too. God is always there. He never says, ‘Not now.’ He always listens. We can pray at any time, in any place.”

Say: “There are many ways to pray. We can say words we have learned, like the Sign of the Cross. We can sing. We can talk to God in our own words: ‘Thank you, God. I am sorry. Please help my friend.’ And we can be quiet, and just be with God, like sitting next to someone you love.”
Say: “Jesus said that when we pray, we should go to a quiet place, and the Father who sees us will hear. He loves it when we talk to him.” (Matthew 6:6)
ask: What is prayer? (Talking to God.)
When can we pray? (Anytime, anywhere.)
What would you like to say to God today? (Let several answer.)
practice: Sit comfortably with eyes closed, or looking at a candle or a crucifix.
Say: “We will be quiet for one minute and think about God.” Keep time.
After one minute, say: “Now say it softly after me: ‘Thank you, God.’ ‘I love you.’”
Let children who want to add their own words do so.
script.close: Sign of the Cross. Say: “God always listens.” Send home: “Pray with your family at bedtime tonight.”

tryit: Be very still for one minute.
Listen in your heart.
Say: “Thank you, God. I love you.”
lessons.saintStory:
Bernadette Soubirous was born in 1844 in the town of Lourdes, France. Her family was very poor, and Bernadette was often sick. She could not read well, but she knew how to pray the Rosary.
In 1858, when she was fourteen, she was gathering firewood near a cave when a beautiful lady appeared to her. The lady held a rosary and smiled. Over the next months, the lady came back eighteen times and asked Bernadette to pray for sinners. Bernadette prayed and obeyed what she was asked. A spring of water began to flow from the cave floor, and many sick people have been healed.
Bernadette became a sister, and she is a saint. She teaches us that anyone can pray, even someone small and poor, and that God hears.

lessons.title: The Our Father
lessons.idea: Jesus taught his friends to pray the Our Father. We pray it every day.
lessons.question: Who do we pray to when we say “Our Father”?
lessons.activity: Learn the Our Father with hand motions, one line at a time.
teach: Aim: the child learns the Our Father as Jesus’ own prayer and begins to say it with understanding. Memorized prayer gives words for a lifetime and ties the child to the whole Church.
The Lord’s Prayer is given by Jesus himself to his disciples and to the Church (CCC 2759, 2765). It makes us children who can say “Our Father” and ask in trust.
Say: “Jesus taught us this prayer to talk to our Father.” Explain “hallowed” as “holy” and “daily bread” as what we need. If asked “Why ‘our’?”: “Because God is Father to all of us together.”

Do not push perfect memorization; mumbling the words is common and fine. Some families say it with different wording (for example, trespasses or debts). Accept the form used at home as well as at church.
Pray it slowly with gestures and note who joins in. Ask “Who taught us this prayer?” and look for “Jesus.” Ask which line they like best.
talk: What do you ask for in the Our Father?
What does “daily bread” mean to you?
Who do you forgive?
quiz: Who taught us the Our Father?|A king|Jesus|A teacher|A saint|1|Matthew 6:9.
The Our Father begins with…|Glory be|Our Father, who art in heaven|Hail Mary|Lord, have mercy|1|CCC 2759.

Why is the Our Father so special?|It is a prayer only for priests|Jesus gave us these very words|It is the first prayer in the Bible|It is a song from long ago|1|Jesus taught his friends the Our Father.
When we say “Our Father,” who are we talking to?|God, our Father in heaven|The priest at Mass|Our own dad at home|The saints in heaven|0|The Our Father speaks to God our Father.
What does “daily bread” mean in the prayer?|Treats for being good|The bread given out at church|A big fancy meal with dessert|What we need each day|3|“Daily bread” means what we need.
lessons.life: Pray the Our Father before meals this week.
lessons.saint: Teresa of Avila: she taught that the Our Father is the best prayer to learn.
lessons.mem: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.
lessons.hook: Say, “Jesus’ friends asked him, ‘Teach us to pray.’ He taught them a special prayer.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to say the first two lines with gestures.

script.open: Ask the children, “If you wanted to ask your friend to teach you to ride a bike, what would you say?” Then, “The friends of Jesus asked him, ‘Lord, teach us to pray.’ And Jesus gave them a prayer.”
teach: Say: “This prayer is called the Our Father. Jesus himself gave us these words, so it is a very special prayer. We pray it at Mass, at home and at school. It begins: ‘Our Father, who art in heaven.’ That means ‘God, you are our Father, and you are in heaven.’”

Go slowly through the parts in simple words. “‘Hallowed be thy name’ means: we say your name with love. ‘Thy kingdom come’ means: may everyone love you. ‘Give us this day our daily bread’ means: please give us what we need. ‘Forgive us our trespasses’ means: forgive us when we do wrong. ‘Deliver us from evil’ means: keep us safe.”
Say: “It is a gift from Jesus. When we pray it, we say Jesus’ own words to God, our Father.”
ask: Who gave us the Our Father? (Jesus.)
Who is the ‘Father’ in this prayer? (God.)
What do we ask God for? (Bread, forgiveness, to be safe.)
practice: Teach one line at a time, with hand motions: “Our Father” (hands up), “who art in heaven” (point up), “hallowed be thy name” (hands folded), “thy kingdom come” (arms wide), “thy will be done” (hand on heart), “give us this day our daily bread” (hands out, cupped), “forgive us our trespasses” (hands on chest), “as we forgive those who trespass against us” (hug yourself), “lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (hold hands out like a shield). Amen.
Repeat each line three times, children copying.
Say the whole prayer slowly with all the motions.
Let a few children lead the group.
script.close: Say the whole prayer one more time, slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say the Our Father with your family at dinner.”

tryit: Say the Our Father one line at a time.
Do the hand motions with the class.
Say it again, very slowly.
lessons.saintStory:
Teresa was born in Avila, Spain, in 1515. When she was a girl she loved to read adventure stories, and she once ran away from home with her brother to find the land of the martyrs. They did not get far. She became a Carmelite nun and spent many years finding it hard to pray.
Later Teresa learned to pray from the heart, and she started new, simple convents where sisters prayed and lived by their faith. She wrote books about prayer, including a book in which she thinks about each line of the Our Father. She is called a Doctor of the Church because she taught so many people how to pray.
Teresa tells us that when we say the Our Father slowly, and think about the words, we are really talking with God.

lessons.title: The Sign of the Cross and Grace
lessons.idea: We begin and end prayer with the Sign of the Cross. We thank God before meals.
lessons.question: What do we say before a meal?
lessons.activity: Practice the Sign of the Cross slowly. Act out a family meal blessing.
teach: Aim: the child gains two prayer habits they can do alone: the Sign of the Cross and a thank-you before eating. Small repeated habits become a prayer life.
The Sign of the Cross begins and ends prayer, naming the Trinity and calling on Christ’s grace (CCC 2157). Grace before and after meals is a traditional rhythm of prayer (CCC 2698).

Say: “The Sign of the Cross tells God we belong to him; Father, Son and Holy Spirit.” If asked “Why three?”: “It’s one God in three persons. It is a mystery we say and love; we don’t need to understand it all.”
Do not scold left–right mix-ups, and mind that Eastern Christians cross themselves right to left. Some homes do not say grace; invite, don’t shame. Avoid hurried “bless-us” rushing.
Practice slowly and watch hands. Ask “Why do we say thank you at meals?” and look for “God gave us food.” See who tries it at snack without a reminder.
talk: Why do we pray before eating?
What are you thankful for?
Who made the food?
quiz: We make the Sign of the Cross to…|Count|Scratch|Wave|Pray in the name of the Trinity|3|CCC 2157.
Before we eat we…|Run|Play|Thank God|Argue|2|Matthew 14:19.
Why do we say grace before meals?|To thank God for our food|To ask for second helpings|Because the cook likes quiet|To let the food cool down a bit|0|We thank God before meals.

What are we praying when we make the Sign of the Cross?|A wish for good luck today|To the Father, Son and Holy Spirit|A greeting to wave at our friends|A way to say goodbye to God|1|The Sign of the Cross is a short prayer of the Trinity.

When is a good time for the Sign of the Cross?|Only when we are scared or sad|Only when a priest is standing near|Only on very special holy days|When we begin and end prayer|3|We begin and end prayer with the Sign of the Cross.
lessons.life: Lead grace at one meal each day this week.
lessons.saint: Brother Lawrence: a kitchen worker who prayed while washing pots.
lessons.mem: Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive. Amen.
lessons.hook: Trace a big cross in the air. “This is how we start our prayers.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to make the Sign of the Cross and say grace.

script.open: Set up a pretend table with plates and cups. Ask, “What do we do before we eat?” Let children say. “Today we’ll learn two things we do every day: the Sign of the Cross, and a prayer before meals.”
teach: Say: “The Sign of the Cross is how a Christian begins to pray. We touch our forehead and say, ‘In the name of the Father.’ We touch our chest and say, ‘and of the Son.’ We touch our left shoulder, then our right, and say, ‘and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.’ We are saying: ‘God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. I belong to him.’”
Say: “The cross is the sign of how much Jesus loves us. He died on a cross for us. When we make the sign of the cross, we remember this.”

Say: “Before we eat, we say thank you to God for our food. We call it grace, because God’s gifts are called graces. We say: ‘Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive, from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen.’”
ask: What do we say when we make the Sign of the Cross? (In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.)
Why do we say grace? (To thank God for food.)
Who gives us our food? (God, through people who work.)
practice: Slowly practice the Sign of the Cross, a part at a time. Use the right hand, touching forehead, chest, left shoulder, right shoulder.
Stand and do it together three times, once very slowly.
Seat children at the pretend table. Say: “We are a family. Let’s say grace.”
Say the grace together, with the Sign of the Cross, then pretend to eat.
script.close: Say the grace together once more. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say grace at dinner tonight.”

tryit: Make the Sign of the Cross slowly.
Act out a family meal blessing.
Say: “Bless us, O Lord.”
lessons.saintStory:
Nicholas Herman was born in France in about 1614. He fought as a soldier when he was young, and then he joined the Carmelites in Paris as a brother, taking the name Lawrence.
Brother Lawrence worked in the monastery kitchen for many years, cooking for the whole community and washing a big pile of dishes. He said that he did not mind. He kept God company while he scrubbed pots and pans, and he called this “practicing the presence of God.” People came to ask him for advice about prayer.
Brother Lawrence teaches us that we can pray anywhere. When we bless our food and begin the day with the Sign of the Cross, even a plain meal turns into a way to talk to God.

units.title: Seasons of the Church
units.eq: How does the year help us follow Jesus?

lessons.title: Advent: waiting for Jesus
lessons.idea: Advent is a time to get ready for Christmas. We light candles on the Advent wreath and wait with joy.
lessons.question: Why do we light candles?
lessons.activity: Make a paper Advent wreath. Add a flame each week.
teach: Aim: the child learns that waiting can be joyful and helps us prepare to welcome Jesus. This counters the idea that Christmas begins in November with shopping.
In Advent the Church recalls the long expectation of the Messiah and renews desire for Christ’s coming (CCC 524). It is a season in the Church year (CCC 1163).
Say: “Advent means getting ready for Jesus. Each candle on the wreath tells us Jesus is nearer.” If asked “Why wait?”: “Good gifts are worth getting ready for, and we get our hearts ready.”
Families may have trees up early or not celebrate. Do not criticize. Avoid making Advent a countdown to gifts. Keep it about kindness, prayer and light, within a five-year-old’s sense of time.
Ask: “How many candles will we light this week? What are we getting ready for?” Look for “Jesus” and a small kind act they plan. See who can name the wreath’s purple and pink.
talk: What are we waiting for?
How can you get your heart ready?
What helps you wait?
quiz: Advent is a time to…|Go to the beach|Fast all day|Prepare for Jesus’s birth|Hunt eggs|2|CCC 524.
The candles of Advent are…|Yellow|Black|Green only|Purple and pink|3|Liturgy.

Why do we light a candle each week in Advent?|To count the days until summer comes|To get ready for Jesus’ birth|Because the church is too dark to see|To say goodbye to Christmas|1|Advent is the time to get ready for Christmas.
What is a good way to get ready in Advent?|Open all our gifts early|Think only about toys we want|Do extra kind things|Stop praying until Christmas|2|We add acts of kindness in Advent.
Is Advent a sad time of waiting?|No, we skip the waiting part|Yes, we hide away until Christmas|No, we wait with joy|Yes, we wait with worry and fear|2|We wait with joy for Jesus.
lessons.life: Light the Advent candle with your family each evening and say a prayer.
lessons.saint: John the Baptist: he told people to get ready for Jesus.
lessons.mem: Come, Lord Jesus.
lessons.hook: Light a purple candle. “We are waiting for something special.”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What do we light in Advent? Why?”

script.open: Bring a calendar with a day circled, or a paper chain with days crossed off. Ask, “Have you ever waited for something exciting, like a birthday? How did you get ready?”
teach: Say: “Advent is the time before Christmas, when we wait for Jesus. It is four weeks long. We use that time to get our hearts ready. Do you clean your room for guests? We make our hearts ready for Jesus.”

Show the wreath: “This is an Advent wreath. It is a circle, which has no end, like God’s love. It has four candles: three purple and one pink. The green branches remind us of life. Each week we light one more candle. The light grows and grows until Christmas.”
Say: “While we wait we pray, ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’ We do kind things. We get ready, like John the Baptist, who said, ‘Get ready, Jesus is coming.’ And we wait with joy.”
ask: What are we waiting for in Advent? (Jesus’ birthday, Christmas.)
How many candles are on the wreath? (Four.)
How can we get ready for Jesus? (Pray, be kind, share.)
practice: Give each child a paper plate (or cut-out ring), green paper, and four candle shapes (three purple, one pink).
Help each child glue the candles on a green wreath.
Color a flame yellow for the first week.
Add one more flame each week, so the wreath grows.
script.close: Say: “Come, Lord Jesus.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Light the Advent wreath with your family.”

tryit: Make a paper wreath with four candles.
Color one flame for this week.
Say: “Come, Lord Jesus.”
lessons.saintStory:
John the Baptist was a cousin of Jesus, born to Elizabeth and Zechariah when they were old. An angel had said that John would get people ready for the Lord.
When John grew up, he lived in the desert, ate locusts and honey, and wore a rough camel-hair cloak. People came from all over to hear him. He told them to be sorry for their sins, share with those in need, and baptize in the Jordan River. He said that someone greater was coming: “I am not worthy to untie his sandals.”
One day Jesus came to John, and John said, “Behold, the Lamb of God.” We hear about John every Advent, because he teaches us how to get ready for Jesus.

lessons.title: Lent and Easter
lessons.idea: Lent is a time to pray and share. Easter is a time of joy because Jesus rose.
lessons.question: How can we share with others?
lessons.activity: Make a Lenten bank for the poor. Decorate an Easter egg with a cross.
teach: Aim: the child sees Lent as a time of loving prayer and sharing and Easter as the greatest joy, because Jesus is alive. Easter, not Lent, is the goal.
Lent is a penitential season of prayer, almsgiving and self-denial (CCC 1438). Easter is the feast of feasts, the Resurrection of Christ (CCC 1169, 540).

Say: “In Lent we pray, share and give up something small to love Jesus more. At Easter, Jesus rose, and we are glad.” If asked “Did Jesus die?”: “Yes, and then he rose to new life. He is alive today.”

Do not dwell on the Crucifixion’s violence. Skip fasting for young children; choose small sacrifices like sharing a toy. Children who have lost a loved one may be sensitive about death; keep Easter hope central.
Ask: “What is one small thing we can do for Lent? What happened at Easter?” Listen for “share”, “pray” and “Jesus is alive.” Notice who greets with Alleluia.
talk: What can you share this Lent?
Why do we celebrate at Easter?
How can you help someone in need?
quiz: Easter is when…|The Church began|Jesus was born|Jesus rose from the dead|The apostles were chosen|2|Luke 24.
In Lent we pray, fast and…|Buy toys|Sleep|Complain|Give to the poor|3|Matthew 6:1-18.
Why is Easter a day of joy?|School is almost out for summer|We finally get to eat treats|Jesus rose from the dead|Spring flowers are blooming everywhere|2|Easter is joyful because Jesus is alive.

Which is a good way to spend Lent?|Complaining about what we gave up|Saving all our things for ourselves|Praying and sharing with others|Hiding away from our friends|2|In Lent we pray, give and share.

We stopped singing “Alleluia” in Lent. What happens at Easter?|We sing it only in a whisper|We sing it again with joy|We keep quiet for the whole year|We forget how the song goes|1|Alleluia returns at Easter.
lessons.life: Put coins in a Lenten box for the poor each week.
lessons.saint: Mary Magdalene: the first person to see Jesus alive on Easter morning.
lessons.mem: Alleluia! Jesus is risen!
lessons.hook: Show a bare branch and a flower. “Lent is quiet. Easter is joyful.”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What do we do in Lent? What do we say at Easter?”

script.open: Start by hiding a toy under a cloth. “I have something to show you, but first we have to wait.” After a minute, lift the cloth. “Waiting makes it even better. The Church does that with Lent and Easter.”
teach: Say: “Lent is the time before Easter. It is forty days. We pray more, we give to those who need help, and we try to say no to things that are not good for us. It is a time to get ready to celebrate that Jesus rose from the dead.”
Tell: “On the first Easter morning, some women went to Jesus’ tomb. The stone was rolled away. The tomb was empty! An angel said, ‘He is not here. He has risen!’ (Luke 24) Jesus was alive!”
Say: “That is why Easter is the happiest day in the whole year. We say ‘Alleluia!’ again, the church is full of flowers, and we celebrate. Lent is a quiet time. Easter is a joyful time.”
ask: What do we do during Lent? (Pray, share, say no to things.)
What happened on Easter morning? (Jesus rose from the dead.)
What is a word we say at Easter? (Alleluia!)
practice: Give each child a small cup or a paper bank. Say: “This is our Lenten bank. When we do something kind or give up a treat, we put in a coin to help the poor.”
Decorate a paper egg with a cross and bright colors.
Hold the eggs up and shout, “Alleluia! Jesus is risen!” Cheer.
Put the eggs on the wall as a bright display.
script.close: Sign of the Cross. Say: “Jesus, thank you for rising for us.” Send home: “Start saving coins for the poor.”

tryit: Put a coin in the Lenten bank each time you share.
Decorate an egg with a cross.
Say: “Alleluia! Jesus is risen!”
lessons.saintStory:
Mary of Magdala was one of the women who followed Jesus and helped to take care of him and his friends. Jesus had set her free from great trouble, and she loved him very much.
She stayed near the cross when most of the friends of Jesus ran away. On the morning of the third day she went to the tomb very early, while it was still dark. The stone had been rolled away, and the tomb was empty. She stood weeping, and then a man spoke her name, “Mary.” She turned and saw it was Jesus! She ran to tell the disciples, “I have seen the Lord!” That is why she is sometimes called the “apostle to the apostles.”
Mary Magdalene shows us what Easter joy is like. The sad time of Lent turned into the greatest news ever told: Jesus is alive.

lessons.title: Ordinary Time and Thank You
lessons.idea: Ordinary Time is the time of green, when we grow like plants in God’s love.
lessons.question: What helps a plant grow?
lessons.activity: Plant seeds in cups and watch them grow. Pray, “Help me grow, Lord.”
teach: Aim: the child learns that ordinary days matter to God and that faith grows slowly. Green for growth supports the idea of daily steady love, not only big feasts.
Ordinary Time is the long stretch of the year when the Church follows Jesus’ life and teaching week by week (CCC 1163, 1168). The year of the Lord is filled with Easter’s light.
Say: “Green is for growing. Every day we grow a little in loving God.” If asked “Why isn’t it special?”: “Every day is a gift from God. Ordinary days are when we practice loving him.”
Avoid implying Ordinary Time is boring or lesser. Gardening comparisons may not fit children without seeds or yards; use windowsill plants. Don’t blame a child whose plant did not grow.
Plant or look at a seed and ask: “How do we grow? Who helps?” Look for answers such as sun, water and God. Notice who offers a thank-you for something small.
talk: What helps a plant grow?
What helps us grow in love?
What are you thankful for?
quiz: Green is the color of…|Easter|Ordinary Time|Lent|Advent|1|Liturgical colors.
We grow in love by…|Prayer and kindness|Fighting|Hiding|Winning|0|Colossians 3.

Why is green the color of Ordinary Time?|It is the color we use for Easter|We grow like plants in God’s love|It is the color we use for sadness|It is the color we use for Christmas|1|Green is the color of growing.

How do we grow in God’s love during Ordinary Time?|By waiting until the next holiday|By trying to be bigger than others|By stopping our prayers for a while|By loving others day by day|3|We grow a little at a time.

Does Ordinary Time mean God is less near?|Yes, only holidays really matter|Yes, God rests until Advent begins|No, but only while we are in church|No, God is with us always|3|God is with us in every season.
lessons.life: Water a plant with your family and thank God for the gift of life.
lessons.saint: Thérèse of Lisieux: she called herself a “little flower” and taught the little way of love.
lessons.mem: Thank you, God, for helping me grow.
lessons.hook: Show a green plant. “Green means growing.”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What color is Ordinary Time? Why?”

script.open: Bring a small plant in a pot and a seed packet. Ask the children, “How does a seed grow?” Take answers (water, sun, soil, time).
teach: Say: “After Christmas and Easter, the Church has a long season called Ordinary Time. The color is green, like grass and leaves. Green is the color of growing. In Ordinary Time we grow, like plants, a little at a time, in God’s love.”
Read Psalm 1:3: “Like a tree planted by streams of water.” Say: “A tree grows tall when it has good water. We grow when we pray, go to Mass, are kind and listen to Jesus.”
Say: “Growing takes time. It does not happen in one day. Every day we can do small things: say a prayer, help someone, say thank you. And God helps us grow, as a gardener cares for the garden.”
ask: What color is Ordinary Time? (Green.)
What does a plant need to grow? (Water, sun, soil.)
What do we need to grow close to God? (Prayer, Mass, kindness.)
practice: Give each child a clear cup, a spoonful of soil and a bean or other seed.
Help children plant their seeds and water them gently.
Write their names on the cups.
Put the cups in a sunny spot and check them each week.
script.close: Say: “Help me grow, Lord.” Say the grace after meals: “We give thee thanks, almighty God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look at your seed and say thank you each day.”

tryit: Plant a seed in a cup.
Water it a little.
Say: “Help me grow, Lord.”
lessons.saintStory:
Thérèse of Lisieux was a young French girl who became a Carmelite nun when she was fifteen. She was not famous or powerful. She felt small, like a little flower in God’s garden.
She wrote that she could not do great things, but she could do small things with great love: smile at a grumpy sister, say thank you, or do a chore quietly. She called this her “little way.” She was very sick for a long time, but kept trusting God. She died when she was twenty-four.
Thérèse is a saint, and a Doctor of the Church. She shows us that in Ordinary Time, when nothing special happens, we can grow in love like a little plant.

units.title: Little hearts, big love
units.eq: What do I do when I make a mistake, when I have a lot, and when I am scared?

lessons.title: Saying sorry and forgiving
lessons.idea: Little children hurt each other and feel bad every day. They need two things: words to say sorry, and the surprise that Jesus always forgives and wants us to forgive. This lesson joins the story of the loving father, the Our Father, and the Sacrament of Penance in the simplest way.
lessons.question: What can you say if you hurt someone?
lessons.activity: Play “Sorry and hug.” Act out a pretend bump or a broken toy. One child says “I am sorry. Can I help?” The other says “I forgive you.” Then both make a heart with their hands.
teach: Aim: the child has words to say sorry and knows Jesus always forgives; forgiving others is learned from being forgiven. This builds the base for Confession and for peacemaking at school.
In the sacrament of Penance God’s mercy pardons the sinner and reconciles him with the Church (CCC 1422–1424). In the Our Father we ask to be forgiven as we forgive (CCC 2842–2845).
Say: “I’m sorry. Please forgive me,” and “I forgive you.” If asked “Does God forgive when I’m not sorry?”: “God always loves us. When we say sorry, we are ready to receive his forgiveness.”
Do not force a premature “I’m sorry.” Insincere apologies teach little; model and invite. Avoid shaming, and watch for children who see themselves as bad. Safety first: report harm to a grown-up.
Role-play a toy-taking scene; ask “What can we say?” Look for a clear apology and an offer to help. See who says “Jesus forgives me” unprompted.

script.open: Hold up a paper heart torn in half. Say, “This heart got broken when someone was unkind. How can we fix it?” Tape it together slowly, and say, “Sorry and forgiving mend hearts.”
teach: Say: “Everyone makes mistakes. Grown-ups too. When we hurt someone, we feel bad inside. Jesus tells us a story about a father whose son went away and made big mistakes. When the son came home, the father ran to hug him. That is how God is with us. He always forgives.”

Say: “When we hurt someone, we can say, ‘I am sorry. Can I help?’ And when someone says sorry to us, we can say, ‘I forgive you.’ We say it in the Our Father too: ‘Forgive us, as we forgive.’ Forgiving means we do not stay angry.”

Say: “If someone keeps hurting you, forgiving does not mean you stay near. Go to a grown-up and tell them. Telling is always okay. And you can tell God too. He is always listening, and he always loves you.”

lessons.saintStory:
Francis lived a long time ago in Italy. He loved God and all God’s creatures. He called the sun his brother and the moon his sister.
One day, the people of a town called Gubbio were afraid of a big wolf. The wolf had been eating their sheep, and no one dared to go outside. Francis went to meet the wolf. He made the sign of the cross and said, “Brother Wolf, come here. Please stop hurting people.”
The story says that the wolf lay down at his feet. Francis made peace between the wolf and the town. The people fed the wolf, and the wolf never hurt anyone again. Francis showed that kindness and peace are stronger than fear.

lessons.title: Thank you, God, and sharing
lessons.idea: Thank-yous and sharing are the first moral habits. Children at five can feel the joy of giving and learn that everything good comes from God. This lesson links the Eucharist as thanksgiving, the Our Father’s daily bread, and the works of mercy in a simple practice.
lessons.question: What are you thankful for today?
lessons.activity: Pass a “thank you ball.” Whoever holds it names one thing they are thankful for. Then place a basket in the middle and each child “gives” a pretend gift to the next, saying “This is for you.”
teach: Aim: the child connects gratitude and sharing with God’s generosity, so giving is joy, not loss. Thankfulness shapes how a child sees the world and the Mass.
Eucharist means thanksgiving (CCC 1328), and every event can become an offering of thanks (CCC 2638). We ask for daily bread, trusting the Father (CCC 2828), and we help the poor (CCC 2443).
Say: “Everything good comes from God, so we say thank you, and we share what we have.” If asked “Why share my toy?”: “Sharing makes both people happy, and it’s how God shares with us.”
Do not force sharing of a special possession or shame the child who hesitates; let them choose. Some families have little. Avoid making thanks a comparison with children who have less.
Ask each child to name one thing they are thankful for and one way to share. Look for a thank-you addressed to God, not just a list. Watch for spontaneous sharing at snack.

script.open: Show a small bag of crackers or blocks. Say, “I have enough for everyone, but only if we share.” Hand them out, and ask, “How did that feel?” Let a few children answer.
teach: Say: “Everything good comes from God: food, family, friends, the sun, the rain. When we say thank you, we remember where good things come from. At Mass we say thank you with Jesus. The word ‘Eucharist’ means thank you.”
Say: “Once, Jesus healed ten sick men. Only one came back to say thank you. Jesus was glad he did. We can be like that one man. We can say thank you to God and to people, every day.”

Say: “Sharing makes joy bigger. A boy had a small lunch, five loaves and two fish. He shared it with Jesus, and Jesus fed five thousand people! Our small gifts are never too small. We share a toy, a snack or a turn. That makes God happy.”

lessons.saintStory:
Zita lived in Italy about eight hundred years ago. When she was twelve she went to work as a servant in a rich house in the city of Lucca. She worked there all her life. She was kind and hard-working, and she loved to pray.
Zita often gave her own food to poor people at the door. Some people in the house were not pleased about this, and even scolded her. One day she was carrying bread in her apron to give away, and was stopped. When she opened her apron, it was full of flowers. People said that God had changed the bread into flowers to protect her.
Another story says she stayed late at church to pray, and when she came back, her bread was already baked. People said angels had done her work. Zita died in 1272, and people in Lucca remembered her as a saint. She is the patron of servants and of people who work at home.

lessons.title: God is with me when I am scared
lessons.idea: Fear in the dark, in a new place, at the doctor or at night is real for five-year-olds. The Church’s teaching on God’s care, the guardian angels, and trust gives simple words and actions: “Jesus, I trust in you,” a guardian angel prayer, and telling a grown-up.
lessons.question: What makes you feel scared? Who helps you?
lessons.activity: Practise a “brave breath”: smell a flower (in), blow out a candle (out). Then say together “Jesus, I trust in you.” Draw a picture of a time you felt scared and a guardian angel standing next to you.
teach: Aim: the child learns that fear is normal, God is near, and there are things to do: breathe, pray, tell a grown-up. This gives real help for nights, doctors and new places.
God cares for each child, whose smallest needs the Father knows (CCC 305). Each person has an angel guardian (CCC 336), and prayer is trust in our Father (CCC 2559).
Say: “God is with you, and your angel too. Say: Jesus, I trust in you.” If asked “Why do scary things happen?”: “Sometimes bad things happen. God is still with us and helps us through them.”
Don’t say “there’s nothing to be afraid of” or shame a child for crying. Some are carrying real fears, like a hospital stay or conflict at home. Pass concerns to parents, and report signs of harm.
Ask: “What can you do when you are scared?” Look for the three steps: breathe, pray, tell a grown-up. Invite a short “Jesus, I trust in you” and see who can say it calmly.

script.open: Dim the lights and sit in a circle. Say, “Sometimes the dark feels scary. Everybody feels scared sometimes.” Then turn on a battery candle. Say, “Look. A little light makes the dark smaller. Jesus is like that light.”
teach: Say: “Feeling scared is normal. Even grown-ups feel scared. But God has not left us alone. Jesus said, ‘I am with you always.’ Always means every day, every night, even when it is dark, and when mom or dad is not in the room.”

Say: “God gave each of us a guardian angel to watch over us. Our angel is with us at home, at school, at night. We can say, ‘Angel of God, my guardian dear.’ And we can say a short prayer: ‘Jesus, I trust in you.’ It is a small prayer, and it is strong.”
Say: “When you feel scared, you can do three things. Take a slow breath. Say, ‘Jesus, I trust in you.’ And tell a grown-up. Telling makes the fear smaller. A grown-up can help you, and so can God.”

lessons.saintStory:
Helena Kowalska was born in 1905 in a small village in Poland, one of ten children. Her family was poor but loved God. She was a quiet, kind girl, and from the time she was young she wanted to be a sister. When she was twenty, she joined a convent and took the name Faustina.
Sister Faustina worked in the kitchen, the garden and at the door of the convent. She said that Jesus appeared to her and asked her to tell the world about his mercy: that he forgives, and that everyone can trust him. She wrote it all down in a diary. She said Jesus asked her to have a picture painted, with the words “Jesus, I trust in you.”
She was often sick, and died in 1938 at the age of thirty-three. Today the picture of Divine Mercy is loved around the world. She was canonized in 2000.
